vocabulary.translation: 自由女神像是自由的标志性象征。

vocabulary.entry: seat of power /siːt ɒv ˈpaʊə(r)/ 权力中心
vocabulary.example: The palace has long been the seat of power in the country.
vocabulary.translation: 这座宫殿长期以来一直是这个国家的权力中心。

vocabulary.entry: city dweller /ˈsɪti ˈdwelə(r)/ 城市居民
vocabulary.example: City dwellers often face problems like traffic jams and air pollution.
vocabulary.translation: 城市居民经常面临交通拥堵和空气污染等问题。

vocabulary.entry: look into /lʊk ˈɪntu/ 调查；研究；回顾
vocabulary.example: The committee will look into the cause of the accident.
vocabulary.translation: 委员会将调查这起事故的原因。

vocabulary.entry: far-flung /ˌfɑː(r) ˈflʌŋ/ adj. 遥远的；偏远的
vocabulary.example: She has traveled to far-flung corners of the world.
vocabulary.translation: 她曾游历过世界上遥远的角落。

vocabulary.entry: establish /ɪˈstæblɪʃ/ v. 建立；设立
vocabulary.example: The company was established in 1990.
vocabulary.translation: 这家公司成立于1990年。

vocabulary.entry: geographical centre /ˌdʒiːəˈɡræfɪkl ˈsentə(r)/ 地理中心
vocabulary.example: The city is located at the geographical centre of the region.
vocabulary.translation: 这座城市位于该地区的地理中心。

vocabulary.entry: exert control /ɪɡˈzɜːt kənˈtrəʊl/ 实施控制；施加影响
vocabulary.example: The government aims to exert better control over the financial market.
vocabulary.translation: 政府旨在更好地控制金融市场。

vocabulary.entry: project unity /prəˈdʒekt ˈjuːnəti/ 彰显团结；展现统一性
vocabulary.example: The national ceremony is designed to project unity among citizens.
vocabulary.translation: 这场国家庆典旨在彰显公民之间的团结。

vocabulary.entry: relocate /ˌriːləʊˈkeɪt/ v. 迁移；重新安置
vocabulary.example: The company decided to relocate its headquarters to a smaller city.
vocabulary.translation: 该公司决定将总部迁至一座较小的城市。

vocabulary.entry: invade /ɪnˈveɪd/ v. 入侵；侵略
vocabulary.example: The army invaded the neighboring country without warning.
vocabulary.translation: 军队毫无征兆地入侵了邻国。

vocabulary.entry: megacity /ˈmeɡəsɪti/ n. 特大城市
vocabulary.example: Mexico City is one of the largest megacities in the world.
vocabulary.translation: 墨西哥城是全球最大的特大城市之一。

vocabulary.entry: sink /sɪŋk/ v. 下沉；下陷
vocabulary.example: The ship began to sink after hitting an iceberg.
vocabulary.translation: 那艘船撞上冰山后开始下沉。

vocabulary.entry: swampy /ˈswɒmpi/ adj. 沼泽的；泥泞的
vocabulary.example: We had to walk through swampy ground to reach the village.
vocabulary.translation: 我们不得不穿过泥泞的沼泽地才能到达那个村庄。

vocabulary.entry: extract groundwater /ɪkˈstrækt ˈɡraʊndwɔːtə(r)/ 抽取地下水
vocabulary.example: Farmers in the area extract groundwater for irrigation.
vocabulary.translation: 该地区的农民抽取地下水用于灌溉。

vocabulary.entry: overcrowded /ˌəʊvəˈkraʊdɪd/ adj. 过度拥挤的
vocabulary.example: The overcrowded train made the journey very uncomfortable.
vocabulary.translation: 拥挤不堪的火车让旅途非常不舒服。

vocabulary.entry: gridlocked /ˈɡrɪdlɒkt/ adj. 交通拥堵的；陷入僵局的
vocabulary.example: The city’s roads are often gridlocked during rush hour.
vocabulary.translation: 这座城市的道路在高峰时段经常陷入交通拥堵。

vocabulary.entry: construct /kənˈstrʌkt/ v. 建造；构建
vocabulary.example: They plan to construct a new bridge across the river.
vocabulary.translation: 他们计划在河上建造一座新桥。

vocabulary.entry: coastal /ˈkəʊstl/ adj. 沿海的；海岸的
vocabulary.example: We spent our holiday in a small coastal town.
vocabulary.translation: 我们在一个海滨小镇度过了假期。

vocabulary.entry: interior /ɪnˈtɪəriə(r)/ n. 内陆；内部
vocabulary.example: The interior of the country is mostly covered with forests.
vocabulary.translation: 这个国家的内陆地区大部分被森林覆盖。

vocabulary.entry: remote /rɪˈməʊt/ adj. 偏远的；遥远的
vocabulary.example: The village is in a remote part of the mountains.
vocabulary.translation: 那个村庄位于山区的偏远地带。

sentences.english: Think of the UK and you’ll probably think of London.
sentences.chinese: 一想到英国，你可能就会想到伦敦。

sentences.english: Picture France and you’ll no doubt conjure up images of Paris and its iconic Eiffel Tower.
sentences.chinese: 一提到法国，毫无疑问你脑海中就会浮现出巴黎和其标志性建筑埃菲尔铁塔的画面。

sentences.english: To many, capital cities define a country.
sentences.chinese: 对许多人来说，首都代表着一个国家。

sentences.english: They’re often the seat of power, the economic and political hub and sometimes the home to royalty - along with millions of city dwellers.
sentences.chinese: 它们通常是权力中心、经济和政治枢纽，有时还是皇室的居所——同时居住着数百万城市居民。

sentences.english: For a place with so much influence, it’s important to get its location right.
sentences.chinese: 对于一个拥有如此大影响力的地方，选址至关重要。

sentences.english: Sometimes we have to look into history to find the reasons why a capital city ended up where it did.
sentences.chinese: 有时我们必须回顾历史，才能找到首都最终定址的原因。

sentences.english: The site of what is now London was by the river: easy to settle, easy for trading and easy to defend.
sentences.chinese: 今天我们所熟知的伦敦紧邻河流：易于定居、便于贸易且易守难攻。

sentences.english: However, it’s not located in the country’s centre and there’s often criticism from far-flung corners of the nation that they are forgotten by the decision makers in the capital.
sentences.chinese: 然而，它并不位于英国的地理中心，因此经常有来自国家偏远地区的批评声音，称他们被首都的决策者所忽视。

sentences.english: Other countries have taken a different approach by establishing their capitals in the geographical centre so they can exert control and project unity, like Madrid in Spain for example.
sentences.chinese: 其他国家则采取了不同的策略，将首都设立在地理中心，以便实施管控并彰显国家统一，例如西班牙的马德里。

sentences.english: Occasionally, there have been reasons to relocate a capital.
sentences.chinese: 偶尔也会有迁移首都的理由。

sentences.english: St Petersburg, founded by Peter the Great in 1703, was Russia’s capital from 1712-1918, before the government changed it to Moscow.
sentences.chinese: 圣彼得堡由彼得大帝于1703年建立，1712年至1918年间一直是俄罗斯的首都，之后政府将首都迁到了莫斯科。

sentences.english: This was partly because Moscow was more central, and the government decided it was less likely to be invaded by another country.
sentences.chinese: 部分原因是莫斯科地理位置更居中，而且政府认为其被他国入侵的风险更低。

sentences.english: And now in Indonesia there are plans to move its capital, Jakarta.
sentences.chinese: 如今，印度尼西亚也计划迁移其首都雅加达。

sentences.english: Its new location is yet to be decided, but the reason for the move is that this megacity is sinking at one of the fastest rates in the world.
sentences.chinese: 新首都的选址尚未确定，但迁移的原因是这座特大城市正以全球最快的速度之一下沉。

sentences.english: It’s been built on very swampy land and isn’t helped by lots of groundwater being extracted to use for drinking water and washing.
sentences.chinese: 雅加达建在一片非常泥泞的沼泽地上，而大量抽取地下水用于饮用和清洗的行为更是加剧了这一问题。

sentences.english: The city is overcrowded too and roads are often gridlocked.
sentences.chinese: 这座城市人口过于拥挤，道路也经常拥堵。

sentences.english: Of course, if you can’t move your capital city, why not construct a brand new one?
sentences.chinese: 当然，如果你无法迁移现有的首都，为什么不新建一座呢？

sentences.english: Brazil moved its capital from coastal, crowded Rio de Janeiro to inland Brasilia in 1961 - the idea being to build a brand new capital "to bring progress to the interior of Brazil", as architect Oscar Niemeyer described it.
sentences.chinese: 1961年，巴西将首都从沿海拥挤的里约热内卢迁至内陆城市巴西利亚——正如建筑师奥斯卡·尼迈耶所描述的那样，建造这座全新首都的初衷是“为巴西内陆地区带来发展”。

sentences.english: And more recently, Nay Pyi Taw was built in 2005 as Myanmar’s new capital.
sentences.chinese: 更近的例子是2005年内比都成为了缅甸的新首都。

sentences.english: This remote city is four times the size of London and has huge roads, golf courses and a zoo – but few people.
sentences.chinese: 这座偏远的城市面积是伦敦的四倍，拥有宽阔的道路、高尔夫球场和动物园——但人口却寥寥无几。

title: Reducing our carbon footprint
paragraphs: For many people, flying is a great way to move quickly and easily from place to place. There are now four billion passengers flying every year. The aviation industry has expanded massively in recent years, with the growth of budget airlines opening up new destinations which we can now reach for peanuts! But this worldwide appetite for travel comes at a price - it’s increasing carbon emissions, which is harming the planet we want to explore.

According to a new study, air travel is one of the things that accounts for eight per cent of carbon emissions – much higher than was first thought. The US tops the rankings followed by China, Germany and India. Dr Arunima Malik from the University of Sydney, who's the lead author of the study, told the BBC that it’s richer people who are more responsible by spending more on high-carbon activities. He says "If you have visitors from high-income countries then they typically spend heavily on air travel, on shopping and hospitality where they go to.”

The World Travel and Tourism Council claims things are changing. A spokesman said "We've seen a growing number of hotels, airports and tour operators that have all become carbon neutral so there is a momentum (to change)." Becoming carbon neutral involves carbon offsetting, where tourists pay extra money in order to contribute to environmental projects that reduce the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere – although some say it's just an excuse to continue polluting. Airline passengers can do this by paying an additional charge when they buy their ticket from participating airlines.

Things are changing and from next year, airlines will be required to offset any increase in emissions beyond their 2020 levels by reducing emissions elsewhere. And there are other ways to reduce your carbon footprint when you take to the skies – you can sit in the cheap seats; studies have shown by flying in business or first class “your emissions are at least three times more than if you decided to travel in economy.” You can also travel from your local airport and pack light – reducing the weight of the aircraft. But some people might say this doesn’t tackle the bigger problem – and the best action is to take a grounded approach and not to fly at all.

vocabulary.entry: aviation industry /ˌeɪviˈeɪʃn ˈɪndəstri/ 航空业
vocabulary.example: The aviation industry has been heavily affected by the global pandemic.
vocabulary.translation: 航空业受到了全球疫情的严重影响。

vocabulary.entry: expand massively /ɪkˈspænd ˈmæsɪvli/ 大规模扩张
vocabulary.example: The technology company has expanded massively in the Asian market.
vocabulary.translation: 这家科技公司在亚洲市场实现了大规模扩张。

vocabulary.entry: budget airlines /ˈbʌdʒɪt ˈeəlaɪnz/ 廉价航空公司
vocabulary.example: Budget airlines have made short-haul flights more affordable for ordinary people.
vocabulary.translation: 廉价航空公司让普通人更能负担得起短途航班。

vocabulary.entry: for peanuts /fɔː ˈpiːnʌts/ 花很少的钱；廉价地
vocabulary.example: You can get a return ticket to the coastal city for peanuts during the off-season.
vocabulary.translation: 淡季时，你花很少的钱就能买到去那座海滨城市的往返机票。

vocabulary.entry: come at a price /kʌm æt ə praɪs/ 付出代价
vocabulary.example: The convenience of online shopping comes at a price of increased packaging waste.

vocabulary.entry: carbon emissions /ˈkɑːbən ɪˈmɪʃnz/ 碳排放
vocabulary.example: Many countries have pledged to cut carbon emissions to combat climate change.
vocabulary.translation: 许多国家承诺减少碳排放以应对气候变化。

vocabulary.entry: account for /əˈkaʊnt fɔː/ 占（比例）；解释
vocabulary.example: Renewable energy now accounts for 20% of the country's total power supply.
vocabulary.translation: 可再生能源目前占该国总供电量的20%。

vocabulary.entry: top the rankings /tɒp ðə ˈræŋkɪŋz/ 位居榜首；排名第一
vocabulary.example: The city tops the rankings for quality of life among European capitals.
vocabulary.translation: 这座城市在欧洲首都的生活质量排名中位居榜首。

vocabulary.entry: high-carbon activities /haɪ ˈkɑːbən ækˈtɪvətiz/ 高碳活动
vocabulary.example: Driving private cars and flying frequently are considered high-carbon activities.
vocabulary.translation: 开私家车和频繁坐飞机被视为高碳活动。

vocabulary.entry: hospitality /ˌhɒspɪˈtæləti/ n. 酒店餐饮服务；好客
vocabulary.example: The hotel is famous for its warm hospitality and excellent service.
vocabulary.translation: 这家酒店以其热情的服务和优质的款待而闻名。

vocabulary.entry: carbon neutral /ˈkɑːbən njuːtrəl/ 碳中和的
vocabulary.example: The company aims to become carbon neutral by 2030 through green initiatives.
vocabulary.translation: 该公司计划通过环保举措在2030年前实现碳中和。

vocabulary.entry: momentum /məˈmentəm/ n. 势头；动力
vocabulary.example: The environmental movement has gained significant momentum in recent years.
vocabulary.translation: 近年来，环保运动获得了强劲的发展势头。

vocabulary.entry: carbon offsetting /ˈkɑːbən ˈɒfsetɪŋ/ 碳抵消
vocabulary.example: Carbon offsetting allows individuals to compensate for their emissions by supporting green projects.
vocabulary.translation: 碳抵消机制让个人可以通过支持环保项目来抵消自己的碳排放。

vocabulary.entry: contribute to /kənˈtrɪbjuːt tu/ 为……做贡献；促成
vocabulary.example: Everyone can contribute to environmental protection by reducing waste.
vocabulary.translation: 每个人都可以通过减少浪费为环保做贡献。

vocabulary.entry: take to the skies /teɪk tu ðə skaɪz/ 坐飞机；启航
vocabulary.example: Thousands of tourists take to the skies during the holiday season.
vocabulary.translation: 假期期间，成千上万的游客选择坐飞机出行。

vocabulary.entry: business class /ˈbɪznəs klɑːs/ 商务舱
vocabulary.example: He upgraded to business class for the long-haul flight to New York.
vocabulary.translation: 他为这趟飞往纽约的长途航班升级到了商务舱。

vocabulary.entry: first class /fɜːst klɑːs/ 头等舱
vocabulary.example: First class passengers enjoy exclusive lounges and personalized service.
vocabulary.translation: 头等舱乘客可以享用专属休息室和个性化服务。

vocabulary.entry: economy (class) /ɪˈkɒnəmi (klɑːs)/ 经济舱
vocabulary.example: Most travelers choose economy class for its affordable prices.
vocabulary.translation: 大多数旅客选择经济舱是因为其价格实惠。

vocabulary.entry: pack light /pæk laɪt/ 轻装出行
vocabulary.example: It's advisable to pack light when traveling by plane to avoid extra baggage fees.
vocabulary.translation: 坐飞机旅行时，轻装出行是明智之举，可以避免额外的行李费。

vocabulary.entry: aircraft /ˈeəkrɑːft/ n. 飞机；航空器
vocabulary.example: The new aircraft is designed to be more fuel-efficient and environmentally friendly.
vocabulary.translation: 这款新飞机设计得更省油、更环保。

vocabulary.entry: tackle the problem /ˈtækl ðə ˈprɒbləm/ 解决问题
vocabulary.example: Governments and businesses must work together to tackle the problem of climate change.
vocabulary.translation: 政府和企业必须携手合作，解决气候变化问题。

vocabulary.entry: grounded approach /ˈɡraʊndɪd əˈprəʊtʃ/ 不坐飞机的方式；务实做法
vocabulary.example: She adopted a grounded approach for her European trip, traveling by train instead of flying.
vocabulary.translation: 她的欧洲之行选择了不坐飞机的方式，而是乘坐火车出行。

sentences.english: For many people, flying is a great way to move quickly and easily from place to place.
sentences.chinese: 对很多人来说，坐飞机是一种方便便捷的出行方式。

sentences.english: There are now four billion passengers flying every year.
sentences.chinese: 如今每年有40亿乘客选择航空出行。

sentences.english: The aviation industry has expanded massively in recent years, with the growth of budget airlines opening up new destinations which we can now reach for peanuts!
sentences.chinese: 近年来，随着廉价航空公司的兴起，航空业实现了大规模扩张，许多新的目的地如今我们花很少的钱就能抵达！

sentences.english: But this worldwide appetite for travel comes at a price - it’s increasing carbon emissions, which is harming the planet we want to explore.
sentences.chinese: 但这种全球范围内的旅行热潮是有代价的——它导致碳排放不断增加，而这正在破坏我们想要探索的地球家园。

sentences.english: According to a new study, air travel is one of the things that accounts for eight per cent of carbon emissions – much higher than was first thought.
sentences.chinese: 一项新研究显示，航空旅行的碳排放量占总排放量的8%，这一比例远高于最初的预估。

sentences.english: The US tops the rankings followed by China, Germany and India.
sentences.chinese: 美国位居榜首，紧随其后的是中国、德国和印度。

sentences.english: Dr Arunima Malik from the University of Sydney, who's the lead author of the study, told the BBC that it’s richer people who are more responsible by spending more on high-carbon activities.
sentences.chinese: 该研究的主要作者、悉尼大学的阿伦尼玛·马利克博士向英国广播公司表示，富人应对此承担更多责任，因为他们在高碳活动上的支出更多。

sentences.english: He says "If you have visitors from high-income countries then they typically spend heavily on air travel, on shopping and hospitality where they go to.”
sentences.chinese: 他说：“如果游客来自高收入国家，他们通常会在目的地的航空旅行、购物和酒店餐饮方面花费重金。”

sentences.english: The World Travel and Tourism Council claims things are changing.
sentences.chinese: 世界旅游及旅行理事会称情况正在发生改变。

sentences.english: A spokesman said "We've seen a growing number of hotels, airports and tour operators that have all become carbon neutral so there is a momentum (to change)."
sentences.chinese: 一位发言人表示：“我们看到越来越多的酒店、机场和旅游运营商实现了碳中和，因此变革的势头已经形成。”

sentences.english: Becoming carbon neutral involves carbon offsetting, where tourists pay extra money in order to contribute to environmental projects that reduce the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere – although some say it's just an excuse to continue polluting.
sentences.chinese: 实现碳中和需要通过碳抵消机制——游客支付额外费用，为减少大气中二氧化碳的环保项目提供资金支持，不过有人认为这只是继续污染的借口。

sentences.english: Airline passengers can do this by paying an additional charge when they buy their ticket from participating airlines.
sentences.chinese: 航空公司乘客可以在参与该机制的航空公司购票时，支付额外费用来参与碳抵消。

sentences.english: Things are changing and from next year, airlines will be required to offset any increase in emissions beyond their 2020 levels by reducing emissions elsewhere.
sentences.chinese: 情况正在发生变化，从明年起，航空公司将被要求通过其他途径减少排放，以抵消超出2020年排放水平的部分。

sentences.english: And there are other ways to reduce your carbon footprint when you take to the skies – you can sit in the cheap seats; studies have shown by flying in business or first class “your emissions are at least three times more than if you decided to travel in economy.”
sentences.chinese: 此外，坐飞机时还有其他减少碳足迹的方法——你可以选择经济舱座位；研究表明，乘坐商务舱或头等舱的“碳排放量至少是选择经济舱的三倍”。

sentences.english: You can also travel from your local airport and pack light – reducing the weight of the aircraft.
sentences.chinese: 你还可以从当地机场出发，并且轻装出行——这样可以减轻飞机重量。

sentences.english: But some people might say this doesn’t tackle the bigger problem – and the best action is to take a grounded approach and not to fly at all.
sentences.chinese: 但有些人可能会说，这些方法并没有解决核心问题，最佳做法是务实的做法——选择不坐飞机的出行方式。

title: Is your lunch costing the earth
paragraphs: A lunch break – it’s an important and often necessary part of our working or school day. It’s a chance to stop your tummy rumbling, grab a bite to eat and maybe chat with some friends. And now we’re spoilt with an array of places to buy our lunch from, all offering tempting dishes and humble sandwiches to eat on the go.

But our appetite for buying our lunchtime fare is not just costing us money, there might be a cost in terms of damaging our planet too. Just grabbing a sandwich, crisps and maybe a cake and coffee can produce at least four items of waste. Cartons, cups, wrappers and plastic cutlery are all part of our disposable feast in addition to the food waste we create. Some experts say throwing away food, which produces methane as it rots, is a bigger cause of climate change than plastics.

But regardless of what causes the most damage, the solution, according to an environmental campaign group called Hubbub, is to eat packed lunches. Tessa Tricks from the group says "People are saying that they are buying food to take out because life has got busier." And she says people think they are being more efficient; but she argues that it’s usually healthier and cheaper to make your own lunch. It means you can eat the things you really want and make the quantity that you actually need.

Of course, preparing your lunch is another thing to fit into your morning scramble of getting ready for work, so if you haven't got time and you are going to buy lunch, an alternative Hubbub suggests is to take your own container to a shop and ask them to put your food in it. The idea of using reusable coffee cups for hot drinks and refilling water bottles has already proved successful, so this could be another step in the right direction. A trial in East Anglia (in the UK) showed that offering a 10% price reduction did persuade some customers to come prepared with their own lunch box.

The problem with eating on the move is that you might want to carry your grub in something that is disposable, so it’s a good idea to make sure it’s something that is recyclable and not to take extra sachets of sauce or utensils that you’re not going to use. The message seems to be that if we give our lunchtime eating habits some thought, we can all do our bit in helping reduce climate change and damage to our environment. That is something for all of us to chew on!

title: Is too much screen time bad for children
titleChinese: 使用屏幕时间过长对儿童有害吗？
paragraphs: If I could have your attention, please. I’d like to talk to you about young people’s screen time. It’s a tempting habit for them to glance at their smartphone or tablet rather than make eye contact with someone and make conversation! There is so much to look at: photographs, social media feeds, messages and emails; it’s no wonder they are glued to their screens. But is it good for them?

There have been many claims about the damage looking at screens does to our eyesight. Some people feared staring at a small bright box could make us short-sighted or lead to headaches. This is a particular concern for children and young people, who spend a higher percentage of time using electronic gadgets. BBC technology correspondent, Rory Cellan-Jones, says: “there is plenty of anecdotal evidence that no matter how long teenagers are spending looking at screens, they are encountering material about issues such as anorexia and self-harm that could prove damaging to their mental health”.

But a new study says time in front of computers and phones might not be as bad for young people as many think. Research by the Oxford Internet Institute examined data from more than 17,000 teenagers in the UK, Ireland and the United States. Their study concluded that most links between life satisfaction and social media use were "trivial", accounting for less than 1% of a teenager's wellbeing. Professor Przybylski, director of research at the institute, said: "99.75% of a person's life satisfaction has nothing to do with their use of social media." The research found that family, friends and school life all had a greater impact on wellbeing.

So, does this mean young people can spend longer looking at social media? The Oxford researchers are confident that their study is robust in its findings and that any correlation between screen time and mental health is very small. Dr Max Davie, officer for health improvement at the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, calls the study a “small first step”, but he said there were other issues to explore, such as screen time's interference with other important activities like sleep, exercise and time with family or friends. Perhaps for now, deciding what the ‘right’ amount of screen time is has to be down to personal judgement.

sentences.chinese: 牛津大学的研究人员对他们的研究结果充满信心，认为屏幕使用时间与心理健康之间的任何关联都非常微弱。

sentences.english: Dr Max Davie, officer for health improvement at the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, calls the study a “small first step”, but he said there were other issues to explore, such as screen time's interference with other important activities like sleep, exercise and time with family or friends.

sentences.english: Perhaps for now, deciding what the ‘right’ amount of screen time is has to be down to personal judgement.

title: Ultra-processed food linked to early death
titleChinese: 食用超加工食品可能导致早逝
paragraphs: It’s good to enjoy food, but sometimes stories about the dangers of eating certain things can be hard to digest. I love to tuck into a pepperoni pizza or munch on a jam doughnut, even though I know the dangers that lurk in their ingredients. It’s clear that processed foods are not the most nutritious things; but there now comes a new threat - from ultra-processed foods.

Scientists have now discovered that eating these types of food - such as chicken nuggets, ice cream and breakfast cereals - have been linked to early death and poor health. This is the stuff that has been through more substantial industrial processing and often has long ingredient lists on the packet, including added preservatives, sweeteners or colour enhancers.

Knowing that your bowl of cornflakes could be bad for you might be hard to swallow, but two studies have shown that people eating more ultra-processed food had worse heart health. Dr Mathilde Touvier from the University of Paris, who conducted one of the studies, told the BBC: "The rapid and worldwide increasing consumption of ultra-processed foods, to the detriment of less processed foods, may drive a substantial burden of cardiovascular diseases in the next decades."

But it might not be completely necessary to change your diet just yet as there is still some uncertainty about the results of the study and questions still to answer. Kevin McConway, a professor of statistics at The Open University, told the BBC: "These studies do increase my confidence that there's something real behind these associations - but I'm still far from sure."

Maybe we should follow the advice of The US National Institutes of Health, which found that ultra-processed foods lead people to eat more and put on more weight. It suggests avoiding food containing ingredients you cannot pronounce or anything your grandmother would not recognise as food! The obvious thing to do seems to be to feast on more unprocessed foods, such as fruit, vegetables, fish, nuts and seeds, beans, lentils and wholegrains, often called a Mediterranean-style diet. After all, we are what we eat!

title: Toy joy!
paragraphs: I’m sure we all have childhood memories – what we did at school, the food we ate, the games we played. But perhaps the most vivid recollections are those of the toys we played with. There were many gadgets that may seem unsophisticated now but were the must-have items in the playground back in the day. Now it seems that our passion for nostalgia means some of them are making a comeback.

One of my favourites was the Nintendo Game Boy, which returned to the shops last year, 30 years after it was first released. This handheld console has had some modifications, but still offers a simple gaming experience and a trip down memory lane! If the Game Boy wasn’t from your era, how about the Tamagotchi? This egg-shaped, plastic pet that its owner had to keep ‘alive’ with constant care and attention - was the must-have item not long after its launch in 1996.

These sometimes annoying ‘creatures’ were such a distraction in the classroom, they often got banned from school. But now, childlike adults can relive their wasted youth because Japanese manufacturer Bandai will soon release an all-colour, new-and-improved version of the classic toy. Its maker says it’s evolved from a pet into more of a character, and can inhabit different lands, as well as get married and breed.

So what’s driving this demand for retro goods? Retail Analyst for Mintel, Chana Baram, told the BBC people are searching for comfort in 'the good old days'. Certainly, playing with an old toy brings back memories of our formative years and gives us a feel-good factor, but it’s also something brands and marketing companies want to cash in on.

Retro toys are also something we could cash in on too. In the darkest corners of many attics and spare rooms lie the toys of Christmas past. And those once much-loved and played with presents may now have a value beyond nostalgia. Toyologist Peter Jenkinson told the BBC that any number of "toys that we all played with as kids are now worth more than a few quid". He suggests there’s a real collectors' market for certain old board games, Star Wars characters, Sindy dolls and Lego sets. However, if you own something like this, it may be just too precious to sell, and part with the connection to your childhood.

title: Could a four-day working week work
titleChinese: 每周四天工作日，可行吗？
paragraphs: People in the UK work longer hours than anyone else in the European Union but are far from the most productive. According to the Trades Union Congress, a UK body that brings together 49 member unions to improve their working conditions, employees in Denmark are 24% more productive per hour but work four hours fewer per week. 'Britain's long-hours culture… is robbing workers of a decent home life and time with their loved ones. Overwork, stress and exhaustion have become the new normal,' says TUC General Secretary Frances O'Grady. They want businesses to cut the standard working week from five days to four. But would a four-day week work?

It does for Rich Leigh, founder of a Gloucester-based PR business. Staff there work Monday to Thursday, 9am – 5:30pm, but still get paid the same as before. In an interview with the BBC, Leigh claims it makes the staff happier, which leads to better, more productive work. After a year, earnings and profits are up and sick days have halved.

The 4 Day Week Campaign also believes a shorter week would benefit everyone. They claim that it would, among other things, more evenly distribute work between the overworked and the underemployed. They estimate that around 30 UK businesses operate a 'four day, same pay' system.

However, not everyone is convinced. One of the UK's leading charities, the Wellcome Trust, conducted an organisation-wide consultation into whether a four-day week would fit. They decided against it. 'Many employees worried about their five-day workloads being compressed into just four days and some raised concerns that the time and energy used to implement a four-day week would distract the charity from its core work,' says Ed Whiting, director of policy at the Trust.

So does a four-day working week work or not? Clearly it suits some… but not everyone. "We've got a lot to do before it can work for different sectors," says Emelia Quist from the Federation of Small Businesses in a BBC interview. 'Social care needs people present 24/7. How can we ensure those industries can work a four-day week?' she adds. Until we can answer questions like these, there's clearly more work to be done.

title: Forest bathing
paragraphs: How do you relax after a stressful day in the office? There are many remedies to help you unwind, but the best solution, according to some experts, lies in the great outdoors. It takes a little effort to get there but the benefits can be a perfect tonic for our stressed out lives. I am talking about the activity of forest bathing.

The Japanese concept of shinrin-yoku – or forest bathing - originates from the 1980s, when it was introduced as a national health programme by the country’s government. Stressed Japanese workers are today still relaxing and reconnecting with nature. The Forest Therapy Society has certified 62 forest therapy sites in the country and the forest bathing movement is also gathering momentum in other parts of the world. It says: "Just as bathing in a hot spring helps to soak your cares away, going for a walk in the woods is said to have a soothing effect."

If you’re worried that bathing involves stripping off your clothes, don’t be! This is about taking time to wander through woodland with no fixed plan or route and just immerse yourself in the forest atmosphere. Some health experts have said that having this exposure to nature seems to promote well-being and that’s particularly good for people with mental health issues. A study conducted in 24 forests across Japan found that walking among trees lowered blood pressure, the pulse rate, and the levels of the hormone cortisol, which is released in response to stress. It also found phytoncides - chemicals emitted by trees - have an anti-microbial effect on humans, boosting our immune systems.

Another study carried out a few years ago by Stanford University in the US, found similar benefits. Brain scans showed reduced activity in an area of the brain linked to the risk of mental illness in participants who took a 90-minute walk among oaks, birds and squirrels. One of the researchers, Gregory Bratman, told the BBC: "There's an increasing body of evidence showing that natural versus urban areas benefit us at least emotionally with our mood and possibly also our cognitive development too.” The evidence seems clear that forest bathing is a shot in the arm for stressed out workers, so now is the time to get out and lose yourself in the natural environment – you could even hug a tree as it could be your new best friend!

sentences.english: The Japanese concept of shinrin-yoku – or forest bathing - originates from the 1980s, when it was introduced as a national health programme by the country’s government.
sentences.chinese: “森林浴”这个日式理念起源于20世纪80年代，当时日本政府将其列为一项国民健康计划。

sentences.english: Stressed Japanese workers are today still relaxing and reconnecting with nature.
sentences.chinese: 如今，承受着压力的日本上班族仍会通过这种方式放松身心，重新亲近自然。

sentences.english: The Forest Therapy Society has certified 62 forest therapy sites in the country and the forest bathing movement is also gathering momentum in other parts of the world.
sentences.chinese: 日本森林疗法协会已经认证了62处森林疗法基地，而森林浴运动也正在世界其他地区逐渐兴起。

sentences.english: It says: "Just as bathing in a hot spring helps to soak your cares away, going for a walk in the woods is said to have a soothing effect."
sentences.chinese: 该协会表示：“就像泡温泉能洗去烦恼一样，在林间漫步据说也能起到舒缓身心的作用。”

sentences.english: If you’re worried that bathing involves stripping off your clothes, don’t be!
sentences.chinese: 如果你担心“浴”意味着要脱掉衣服，那大可不必！

sentences.english: This is about taking time to wander through woodland with no fixed plan or route and just immerse yourself in the forest atmosphere.
sentences.chinese: 森林浴的核心是花时间在林间漫步，不设定固定的计划或路线，只需全身心沉浸在森林的氛围中。

sentences.english: Some health experts have said that having this exposure to nature seems to promote well-being and that’s particularly good for people with mental health issues.
sentences.chinese: 一些健康专家称，这种亲近自然的方式似乎能提升幸福感，尤其对存在心理健康问题的人群有益。

sentences.english: A study conducted in 24 forests across Japan found that walking among trees lowered blood pressure, the pulse rate, and the levels of the hormone cortisol, which is released in response to stress.
sentences.chinese: 一项在日本24片森林中开展的研究发现，在林间行走能降低血压、心率，以及应激激素皮质醇的水平。

sentences.english: It also found phytoncides - chemicals emitted by trees - have an anti-microbial effect on humans, boosting our immune systems.
sentences.chinese: 研究还发现，树木释放的化学物质——植物杀菌素，对人体具有抗菌作用，能增强我们的免疫系统。

sentences.english: Another study carried out a few years ago by Stanford University in the US, found similar benefits.
sentences.chinese: 美国斯坦福大学几年前开展的另一项研究也得出了类似的结论。

sentences.english: Brain scans showed reduced activity in an area of the brain linked to the risk of mental illness in participants who took a 90-minute walk among oaks, birds and squirrels.
sentences.chinese: 脑部扫描结果显示，漫步于阵阵鸟鸣和松鼠穿梭的橡树间90分钟，参与者大脑中与精神疾病风险相关的区域活跃度有所降低。

sentences.english: One of the researchers, Gregory Bratman, told the BBC: "There's an increasing body of evidence showing that natural versus urban areas benefit us at least emotionally with our mood and possibly also our cognitive development too.”
sentences.chinese: 研究人员之一格雷戈里·布拉特曼向英国广播公司表示：“越来越多的证据表明，与城市环境相比，自然环境至少能在情绪层面让我们受益，改善心情，甚至可能对认知发展也有帮助。”

sentences.english: The evidence seems clear that forest bathing is a shot in the arm for stressed out workers, so now is the time to get out and lose yourself in the natural environment – you could even hug a tree as it could be your new best friend!
sentences.chinese: 证据似乎很明确，森林浴对压力缠身的上班族来说是一剂强心针。所以，现在就走出家门，沉浸在自然环境中吧——你甚至可以拥抱一棵树，就像它会成为你最好的新朋友！

title: Dogs helping stressed out students
paragraphs: Some people say that dogs are man’s best friend – good companions, loyal and loveable. Of course, they can be more than just a pet as certain breeds are excellent working dogs too. We know about the amazing help guide dogs give to blind people and, more recently, a new role has been found for the animals – working as therapy dogs in universities.

Research by Washington State University in the US, has found spending time with a pooch can help stressed out students. Patricia Pendry from the university told the BBC that a study of 300 undergraduates had found weekly hour-long sessions with dogs brought to the university by professional handlers had made stressed students at "high risk of academic failure" or dropping out, "feel relaxed and accepted". The dogs helped them to concentrate, learn and remember information.

I know that stroking a dog helps me to relax; other research has shown that petting animals can reduce stress hormone levels and anxiety, so it makes sense to introduce them into an environment where people are stressed. The BBC’s education correspondent Sean Coughlan writes that around 1,000 campuses in the US already use therapy pets and it’s becoming more common in the UK. For example, The University of Middlesex has employed ‘canine teaching assistants’ to help stop lonely students dropping out. Fiona Suthers, head of clinical skills at the university, says that five Labradors had a “stringent assessment” to ensure they had the right temperament. But she adds “it’s hard to describe the impact of just having a dog lying down in the corner of a class.”

Using dogs for therapy can also help the dogs themselves. In Wales, Swansea University Students’ Union has used rescued greyhounds to help students unwind between exams. Sessions allow mistreated and abandoned dogs to interact with humans and begin to trust them again. Student Union education officer Chloe Hutchinson told the BBC that “a lot of students have dogs at home and might be a bit homesick, especially around exam time when it is stressful and you just want your home comforts.” So if you’re a student who’s been working like a dog, but you still feel like you haven’t a dog’s chance in passing your exams, maybe introducing a four-legged friend into your life might be the help you need.

title: The future of pocket money
paragraphs: There are many things we remember from our childhood – the games we played, the music we listened to; but what about earning pocket money? This was our first ever wage for completing tasks such as tidying our bedroom or sorting the laundry. Our reward was a handful of coins that we safely stashed away. But now, it seems, parents’ attitude to handing out cash is changing.

There was a time when cash was king – it was the main currency for financial transactions. These days, though, using credit or debit cards, or making contactless payments, are the most convenient ways of paying. So where does that leave handing over pocket money? Research has found that 84% of British parents currently give notes and coins to their children - typically an allowance, including some discretionary spending, of £7 a week.

But banks predict that by 2028 only one in ten transactions will be with cash, and that it's something today’s children will have to deal with. One particular issue is that children may not understand the value of cash because they never see it. Parents face a dilemma too – finding a new way to transfer pocket money, or maybe not bothering to pay it at all.

Giving children lessons about finance at school is important, and the UK’s Money and Pensions Service advises parents to get children started with money as young as possible. Sarah Porretta from the service told the BBC that for parents who no longer carry cash “The trick is to go and get some coins, just so your children have the opportunity to interact with them. Talk about what you are doing with money. If you are paying with a card or with a phone, talk to children about that and link it back to those coins they have handled."

But, of course, many of the goods that young people want to buy – such as add-ons for a computer game – only allow digital transactions. This has led to a number of apps being set up that allow children to track and spend their hard-earned pocket money and parents to transfer money electronically and monitor their child’s spending. Banks also suggest setting up accounts for older children which gives them a cash card to use. But whatever method a parent chooses to adopt, they need to teach their kids that money doesn’t grow on trees!

sentences.chinese: 那是我们完成整理卧室、分拣衣物这类家务所获得的人生中第一份劳动报酬。

sentences.english: Our reward was a handful of coins that we safely stashed away.
sentences.chinese: 我们会把得到的几枚硬币小心翼翼地存起来。

sentences.english: But now, it seems, parents’ attitude to handing out cash is changing.
sentences.chinese: 但如今，父母们给孩子现金零花钱的态度似乎正在发生改变。

sentences.english: There was a time when cash was king – it was the main currency for financial transactions.
sentences.chinese: 曾经有一段时期，现金为王——它是金融交易的主要支付方式。

sentences.english: These days, though, using credit or debit cards, or making contactless payments, are the most convenient ways of paying.
sentences.chinese: 但如今，使用信用卡、借记卡或者非接触式支付，成了最便捷的付款途径。

sentences.english: So where does that leave handing over pocket money?
sentences.chinese: 那么，这对现金零花钱的发放会产生什么影响呢？

sentences.english: Research has found that 84% of British parents currently give notes and coins to their children - typically an allowance, including some discretionary spending, of £7 a week.
sentences.chinese: 研究发现，目前84%的英国家长仍会给孩子纸币和硬币作为零花钱，每周的金额通常为7英镑，其中包含一部分可自由支配的开支。

sentences.english: But banks predict that by 2028 only one in ten transactions will be with cash, and that it's something today’s children will have to deal with.
sentences.chinese: 但银行预测，到2028年，只有十分之一的交易会使用现金，这是如今的孩子们未来必须面对的情况。

sentences.english: One particular issue is that children may not understand the value of cash because they never see it.
sentences.chinese: 一个尤为突出的问题是，孩子们可能会因为从未接触过现金，而无法理解它的价值。

sentences.english: Parents face a dilemma too – finding a new way to transfer pocket money, or maybe not bothering to pay it at all.
sentences.chinese: 家长们也面临着两难境地——要么寻找发放零花钱的新方式，要么干脆不再给孩子零花钱。

sentences.english: Giving children lessons about finance at school is important, and the UK’s Money and Pensions Service advises parents to get children started with money as young as possible.
sentences.chinese: 在学校对孩子进行金融知识启蒙十分重要，英国货币与养老金服务机构建议家长尽早培养孩子的金钱观念。

sentences.english: Sarah Porretta from the service told the BBC that for parents who no longer carry cash “The trick is to go and get some coins, just so your children have the opportunity to interact with them.
sentences.chinese: 该机构的萨拉·波雷塔向英国广播公司表示，对于那些不再随身携带现金的家长来说，“办法就是去兑换一些硬币，让孩子有机会接触它们。

sentences.english: Talk about what you are doing with money. If you are paying with a card or with a phone, talk to children about that and link it back to those coins they have handled."
sentences.chinese: 和孩子聊聊你是如何使用金钱的，如果你用银行卡或手机支付，也要跟孩子解释清楚，并把这种支付方式和他们使用过的硬币联系起来。”

sentences.english: But, of course, many of the goods that young people want to buy – such as add-ons for a computer game – only allow digital transactions.
sentences.chinese: 当然，年轻人想买的很多东西——比如电脑游戏的附加内容——只支持数字支付。

sentences.english: This has led to a number of apps being set up that allow children to track and spend their hard-earned pocket money and parents to transfer money electronically and monitor their child’s spending.
sentences.chinese: 这催生了多款相关应用程序，孩子们可以通过这些应用记录和使用自己辛苦赚来的零花钱，家长则可以通过电子转账的方式发放零花钱，并监控孩子的消费情况。

sentences.english: Banks also suggest setting up accounts for older children which gives them a cash card to use.
sentences.chinese: 银行还建议为年龄稍大的孩子开设账户，为他们办理现金卡。

sentences.english: But whatever method a parent chooses to adopt, they need to teach their kids that money doesn’t grow on trees!
sentences.chinese: 但无论家长选择哪种方式，都需要告诉孩子：钱不是大风刮来的！

title: Electric scooter safety
paragraphs: If you look around the streets of London, you’ll see the many methods people use to move around. Whether it’s on a commute to work, a trip to the shops, or a sightseeing excursion, there are people on buses, the Tube, cars, motorbikes, bicycles and even roller skates. The roads are already congested; and now there’s a new addition: electric, or 'e-scooters'.

This traditional children’s vehicle has become more sophisticated over the years. And now, with the addition of a small electric motor, it’s become a cheap and easy mode of transport. Scooting around town can be fun and doesn’t involve much effort, so it’s no wonder they’re becoming increasingly popular in cities around the world. But following what’s believed to be the first fatal accident involving an electric scooter in the UK, questions are being asked about their safety and whether traffic laws should be changed.

Some scooter riders have been seen on pavements; others on the road jumping red traffic lights, adding to the frustration of motorists stuck in jams. In the UK, the law states that riding one on the public highway or pavement is forbidden. Riders currently face a £300 fixed-penalty notice and six points on their driving licence for doing so. But, despite this, it seems the increasing popularity of e-scooters means they can be seen everywhere. And now users are calling on regulations to be changed.

The UK government is looking at how safely they can be used on the road and is ‘reviewing’ the law. But its transport minister, Michael Ellis, has told the BBC that: "Micromobility products are appearing in countries across the globe and are an exciting innovation for which we know there is demand. However, safety must always be our top priority when considering their use on public highways in this country.”

There’s no doubt there are dangers in riding a two-wheeled scooter. Despite the fact that some of them can exceed 30mph, they sometimes only have one brake and no lights. They also become unstable if the rider hits a pothole, and however confident the rider may be, larger vehicles on the road make them vulnerable. So it seems more work needs to be done to give e-scooters a safe and legal space to travel in.

title: A pay rise please!
paragraphs: Being an employee at a company has many challenges – you want job satisfaction, a work-life balance and opportunities for promotion. But most of us want a decent financial reward. We aim to get a good salary to pay for the essential things in life plus a few luxuries. But when that’s not enough, we have to do the hardest thing in the world – ask our boss for a pay rise!

In some companies, a regular annual pay rise is the norm – all staff get a fixed increase in their monthly pay packet. In other firms, workers might get a bonus to reward them for their efforts or for meeting a target. But for some people, a pay increase is something you have to ask for – and if you don’t ask, you don’t get!

Wage increases have been a sensitive issue in recent years. Due to the global economic recession, businesses had to tighten their belts. Most public sector pay in the UK, for example, was frozen for two years in 2010, and after that rises were capped at 1% - below the rate of inflation. But last month the government awarded them a pay rise above the 2% inflation rate so that teachers, for example, will get a 2.75% salary boost. That's the equivalent to £1,000 extra a year for those on an average salary.

But not everyone is happy at being given a fixed pay rise – they feel they’re worth more and that they deserve more money. It’s not something we should fear “asking for”, says Pip Jamieson, founder of the professional networking site, The Dots. She’s told the BBC “No one ever got fired for asking for a pay rise. In fact, rather the opposite - asking for more money shows ambition and shows you want to stay with the company.”

It’s something BBC Business Reporter Jamie Robertson has been looking into. He’s found that you need to do your research and find out what kind of pay your job should be getting, perhaps by talking to your Human Resources department. You’ll need to give good reasons for wanting more money and you’ll still have to keep your increase within your pay grade. Ask for an exact sum and be prepared for some negotiation. Of course, if you can’t get more cash then there are other perks you could ask for, such as flexible working or more time off. But if that gets you nowhere and your boss won’t budge, maybe it’s time to quit and find a new job?

sentences.english: In some companies, a regular annual pay rise is the norm – all staff get a fixed increase in their monthly pay packet.

sentences.chinese: 比如在英国，2010年大多数公共部门的薪资两年内毫无变化，在那之后，薪资涨幅最高也没有超过1%，这一比例低于通货膨胀率。

sentences.chinese: 但上个月，政府为公共部门员工提供了高于2%通胀率的加薪幅度，以教师为例，他们的薪资将上涨2.75%。

sentences.chinese: 对于平均薪资水平的人来说，这相当于每年多收入1000英镑。

sentences.chinese: 但并非所有人都满足于固定幅度的加薪——他们认为自己的价值更高，理应获得更多报酬。

sentences.english: It’s not something we should fear “asking for”, says Pip Jamieson, founder of the professional networking site, The Dots.
sentences.chinese: 职业社交网站The Dots的创始人皮普·詹米森表示，要求加薪这件事根本无需畏惧。

sentences.english: She’s told the BBC “No one ever got fired for asking for a pay rise.
sentences.chinese: 她在接受BBC采访时说：“从来没有人会因为要求加薪而被解雇。

sentences.chinese: 事实上，恰恰相反——主动要求加薪彰显了你的抱负，也表明你希望继续留在公司发展。”

sentences.english: It’s something BBC Business Reporter Jamie Robertson has been looking into.
sentences.chinese: BBC商业记者杰米·罗伯逊一直在研究这件事。

sentences.chinese: 他发现，你需要先做些功课，弄清楚自己的岗位应得的薪资水平，或许可以咨询人力资源部门。

sentences.english: You’ll need to give good reasons for wanting more money and you’ll still have to keep your increase within your pay grade.
sentences.chinese: 你需要给出加薪的充分理由，而且加薪幅度还得在自己的薪资等级范围内。

sentences.chinese: 提出明确的加薪数额，并做好谈判的准备。

sentences.english: But if that gets you nowhere and your boss won’t budge, maybe it’s time to quit and find a new job?

title: Who’s still smoking
paragraphs: If you walked into a cafe or pub in the UK a few years ago, chances were you’d enter a room filled with cigarette smoke. The aroma of burning tobacco lingered on your clothes for the rest of day and your health took a battering from passive smoking. It’s no wonder that in many countries smoking in public places has now been banned, and those who choose to do it have to inhale on the pavements outside.

Laws restricting where people can light up and repeated health warnings have seen many people quit the habit. But despite a decline in smoking rates worldwide, a report published in the medical journal The Lancet in 2017 found that smoking causes one in ten deaths worldwide, half of them in just four countries - China, India, the US and Russia.
When population growth is taken into account, there is actually an increase in the overall number of smokers. So why - despite the warning signs - are these people still doing it?

Much of it seems to be connected to people’s cultural, economic and social background. In the UK, for example, the Office for National Statistics found that people living on a low income are disproportionately likely to smoke. And one in four manual workers smokes, compared with one in ten of those in professional or managerial jobs. Dr Leonie Brose from King's College London, writing about this for the BBC, says there are “startling” regional variations with many more pregnant women smoking in deprived areas. And people with mental health problems are “50% more likely to smoke than the rest of the population”. She suggests these groups can have higher levels of dependence, making it harder to give up and are also more likely to be around other smokers, making it seem like normal behaviour.

Increasing the price of cigarettes and making packaging plainer are two ways to discourage smoking; and lower-risk nicotine patches and e-cigarettes are available as an alternative, though they can be just as addictive. It’s obvious something needs to be done and recently the UK government pledged to end smoking in England by 2030 as part of a range of measures to tackle the causes of preventable ill health. But as Dr Leonie Brose writes, “with more than 200 deaths in England per day [caused by smoking-related diseases,] that’s the equivalent to a plane crashing every day.” Imagine what the number must be globally.

title: Tourism controls
titleChinese: 世界著名景点为控制游客数量出新招
paragraphs: I love holidays! There’s nothing better than jetting off to a foreign destination to visit the attractions it has on offer. Of course, I’m not alone. Millions of people are doing the same, and why not? The world has an amazing variety of must-see sights, from breathtaking natural scenery to impressive old cities. But the problem is that too many of us are visiting them at the same time, putting pressure on these delicate and ancient places.

That’s why a number of beauty spots and historic sites have been introducing charges or restrictions on the tourists who visit. There are many reasons for this: to reduce overcrowding, which can spoil the ambience of a place, to manage wear and tear on old crumbling buildings, to tidy up the mess that visitors leave behind, or – as some may suggest – creating tourist traps to make more money out of the visitors.

The famous Italian city of Venice with its picturesque canals has, for example, introduced an entry fee of up to €10 for short-stay tourists. Venetians have long complained that mass tourism is swamping the city. Now, passengers arriving by cruise ship will have to pay a ‘landing tax’ which Mayor Luigi Brugnaro says, “would generate much-needed income to keep the city clean.”

Many cities in Europe already charge an occupancy tax on tourists who stay in hotels and guest houses. In the UK, Edinburgh is hoping to do the same, controversially making it the first city in the country to do so. This levy, that is usually charged per person per night of accommodation, raises money to help protect the environment, pay for infrastructure, or promote tourism.

In Italy’s capital city, Rome, new laws are being introduced to clampdown on bad tourist behaviour, which some argue is spoiling the look and feel of the city. Rules include banning drinking water from fountains and attaching ‘love padlocks’ to bridges.
As more of us can now afford to travel, tourist destinations are going to get busier, so maybe new laws and taxes are going to be a necessary part of the sightseeing experience.

vocabulary.entry: tourist trap /ˈtʊərɪst træp/ 旅游陷阱（指宰游客的场所）

vocabulary.translation: 那家纪念品商店就是个十足的旅游陷阱，价格高得离谱。

vocabulary.entry: picturesque /ˌpɪktʃəˈresk/ adj. 风景如画的；别致的
vocabulary.example: We stayed in a picturesque village in the Lake District.
vocabulary.translation: 我们住在湖区一个风景如画的村庄里。

vocabulary.entry: mass tourism /mæs ˈtʊərɪzəm/ 大规模旅游业
vocabulary.example: Mass tourism has had a huge impact on the small coastal town.
vocabulary.translation: 大规模旅游业给这座海滨小镇带来了巨大影响。

vocabulary.entry: swamp /swɒmp/ v. 淹没；使应接不暇
vocabulary.example: The office was swamped with applications for the job.
vocabulary.translation: 办公室收到了大量的这份工作申请书，应接不暇。

vocabulary.entry: cruise ship /ˈkruːz ʃɪp/ 游轮；邮轮
vocabulary.example: Thousands of tourists arrive at the port by cruise ship every summer.
vocabulary.translation: 每年夏天都有成千上万的游客乘坐游轮抵达这座港口。

vocabulary.entry: occupancy tax /ˈɒkjəpənsi tæks/ 住宿税
vocabulary.example: The city council plans to introduce an occupancy tax on all hotel rooms.
vocabulary.translation: 市议会计划对所有酒店客房征收住宿税。

vocabulary.entry: levy /ˈlevi/ n. 税款；征收额
vocabulary.example: The government imposed a levy on imported goods.
vocabulary.translation: 政府对进口商品征收了一项税款。

vocabulary.entry: infrastructure /ˈɪnfrəstrʌktʃə/ n. 基础设施
vocabulary.example: The country needs to invest more in transport infrastructure.
vocabulary.translation: 该国需要在交通基础设施上投入更多资金。

vocabulary.entry: clampdown on /ˈklæmpdaʊn ɒn/ 严厉打击；严格管控
vocabulary.example: The police are planning a clampdown on illegal parking.
vocabulary.translation: 警方计划严厉打击违章停车行为。

vocabulary.entry: love padlock /ˈlʌv pædlɒk/ 爱情锁
vocabulary.example: Couples often attach love padlocks to the bridge to symbolize their relationship.
vocabulary.translation: 情侣们常常在桥上挂爱情锁，以此象征他们的恋情。

sentences.english: I love holidays!
sentences.chinese: 我热爱假期！

sentences.english: There’s nothing better than jetting off to a foreign destination to visit the attractions it has on offer.
sentences.chinese: 没有什么比搭乘飞机前往异国他乡，游览当地的特色景点更惬意的事了。

sentences.english: Of course, I’m not alone.
sentences.chinese: 当然，并非只有我这么想。

sentences.english: Millions of people are doing the same, and why not?
sentences.chinese: 成千上万的人都在做着同样的事，为什么不呢？

sentences.english: The world has an amazing variety of must-see sights, from breathtaking natural scenery to impressive old cities.
sentences.chinese: 世界上有各种各样不容错过的景观，从令人惊叹的自然风光到宏伟的古城。

sentences.english: But the problem is that too many of us are visiting them at the same time, putting pressure on these delicate and ancient places.
sentences.chinese: 但问题在于，太多人选择在同一时间前往这些地方，给这些脆弱而古老的景点带来了巨大压力。

sentences.english: That’s why a number of beauty spots and historic sites have been introducing charges or restrictions on the tourists who visit.
sentences.chinese: 这也是为什么许多风景名胜和历史古迹开始对游客收取费用或设置游览限制。

sentences.english: There are many reasons for this: to reduce overcrowding, which can spoil the ambience of a place, to manage wear and tear on old crumbling buildings, to tidy up the mess that visitors leave behind, or – as some may suggest – creating tourist traps to make more money out of the visitors.
sentences.chinese: 这么做的原因有很多：缓解拥挤——毕竟拥挤会破坏氛围；减少对老旧建筑的损耗；清理游客留下的脏乱垃圾；或者，正如有些人猜测的那样，打造“旅游陷阱”来从游客身上榨取更多利润。

sentences.english: The famous Italian city of Venice with its picturesque canals has, for example, introduced an entry fee of up to €10 for short-stay tourists.
sentences.chinese: 以拥有如画运河的意大利名城威尼斯为例，该市已开始向短途游客征收最高10欧元的入城费。

sentences.english: Venetians have long complained that mass tourism is swamping the city.
sentences.chinese: 威尼斯人长期以来一直抱怨，大规模的旅游业正在淹没这座城市。

sentences.english: Now, passengers arriving by cruise ship will have to pay a ‘landing tax’ which Mayor Luigi Brugnaro says, “would generate much-needed income to keep the city clean.”
sentences.chinese: 如今，乘坐游轮抵达的游客还需要缴纳“上岸税”，市长路易吉·布鲁尼亚罗表示，这笔税款“将为城市保洁工作带来急需的收入”。

sentences.english: Many cities in Europe already charge an occupancy tax on tourists who stay in hotels and guest houses.
sentences.chinese: 欧洲的许多城市早已开始对入住酒店和民宿的游客征收住宿税。

sentences.english: In the UK, Edinburgh is hoping to do the same, controversially making it the first city in the country to do so.
sentences.chinese: 在英国，爱丁堡市也计划推行这项政策，这一举措颇具争议，若落地，爱丁堡将成为英国首个征收游客住宿税的城市。

sentences.english: This levy, that is usually charged per person per night of accommodation, raises money to help protect the environment, pay for infrastructure, or promote tourism.
sentences.chinese: 这种税费通常按每人每晚的住宿费来收取，所筹集的资金将被用于环境保护、基础设施建设或旅游业推广。

sentences.english: In Italy’s capital city, Rome, new laws are being introduced to clampdown on bad tourist behaviour, which some argue is spoiling the look and feel of the city.
sentences.chinese: 在意大利首都罗马，政府出台了新法规来打击不文明的游客行为——有人认为这类行为正在破坏这座城市的风貌。

sentences.english: Rules include banning drinking water from fountains and attaching ‘love padlocks’ to bridges.
sentences.chinese: 新规包括禁止饮用喷泉里的水，以及禁止在桥上悬挂“爱情锁”。

sentences.english: As more of us can now afford to travel, tourist destinations are going to get busier, so maybe new laws and taxes are going to be a necessary part of the sightseeing experience.
sentences.chinese: 随着越来越多的人有能力外出旅行，旅游目的地会变得愈发拥挤，或许新的法规和税费政策，将成为观光体验中必不可少的一部分。

title: The problem with fast fashion
paragraphs: There's nothing quite like new clothes, is there? The UK certainly loves them. According to a report by the Environmental Audit Committee (EAC), the UK consumes five times more clothes today than it did in the 1980s. That's more than any other nation in Europe and amounts to around 26.7kgs per person. This results in 235 million garments going to landfill – victims of fast fashion.

Fast fashion is defined as “an accelerated fashion business model” involving “increased numbers of new fashion collections every year”, “quick turnarounds” and “lower prices”, according to the EAC. Globalisation means that attire is made in countries where labour is cheaper. This saving is passed on to consumers, who then consider the garb they own disposable – easily replaceable with something more on-trend. And that creates problems.

First, there's the environmental cost. Manufacturing any kind of textile costs resources. For example, synthetic fibres, which are made from plastic, have a larger carbon footprint than natural ones. Natural fibres, although more carbon-efficient, still require more water to grow. And further resources are used as the cloth is dyed, made into clothing and transported to retail for sale. Secondly, the fast-fashion industry is under pressure to put the latest trending items on shelves fast, which can lead to workers being exploited and forced to labour in poor working conditions. In countries such as Bangladesh, Ethiopia and the Philippines, workers are paid wages that are insufficient to live on. One worker in Ethiopia told the BBC that they had to deal with intolerable conditions, such as withheld overtime payments, verbal abuse, and unsanitary toilets.

So what can be done in the UK to reduce clothes waste? The EAC has recommended eighteen improvements to the UK government, from increasing tax on purchases to fund recycling centres to introducing more sewing lessons in schools, encouraging a make do and mend attitude when things become threadbare.

What can we do? Shop “second-hand and vintage,” recommends Tolly Gregory, an ethical fashion blogger. Kristabel Plummer, a London-based fashion blogger, who spoke to the BBC, also recommends “looking for quality” and “longevity”. So keep an eye out for durable, resilient, hardy apparel that resists wear and tear.

vocabulary.example: Too much waste is being sent to landfill.

vocabulary.example: She wore formal attire to the wedding.
vocabulary.translation: 她穿着正装参加婚礼。

vocabulary.example: The actors were in historical garb for the play.
vocabulary.translation: 演员们穿着古装出演这出戏。

vocabulary.example: These are disposable face masks for daily use.
vocabulary.translation: 这些是日常使用的一次性口罩。

vocabulary.entry: on-trend /ɒn trend/ adj. 时髦的；符合潮流的

vocabulary.translation: 她的穿着总是很时髦。

vocabulary.entry: textile /ˈtekstaɪl/ n. 纺织品

vocabulary.translation: 棉花和羊毛是常见的天然纺织品。

vocabulary.entry: synthetic fibre /sɪnˈθetɪk ˈfaɪbə(r)/ 合成纤维
vocabulary.example: Polyester is a type of synthetic fibre.
vocabulary.translation: 聚酯纤维是一种合成纤维。

vocabulary.entry: natural fibre /ˈnætʃrəl ˈfaɪbə(r)/ 天然纤维
vocabulary.example: Silk is a highly prized natural fibre.
vocabulary.translation: 丝绸是一种备受珍视的天然纤维。

vocabulary.entry: dye /daɪ/ v. 染色
vocabulary.example: They use plant extracts to dye the fabric.
vocabulary.translation: 他们用植物提取物给布料染色。

vocabulary.entry: exploit /ɪkˈsplɔɪt/ v. 剥削
vocabulary.example: Some companies exploit workers by paying low wages.
vocabulary.translation: 一些公司通过支付低工资来剥削工人。

vocabulary.entry: insufficient to live on /ˌɪnsəˈfɪʃnt tu lɪv ɒn/ 不足以维持生计
vocabulary.example: The salary is insufficient to live on in this expensive city.
vocabulary.translation: 在这座消费高昂的城市，这份工资不足以维持生计。

vocabulary.entry: withhold /wɪðˈhəʊld/ v. 克扣；扣留

sentences.english: Natural fibres, although more carbon-efficient, still require more water to grow.
sentences.chinese: 而天然纤维虽然更低碳，但种植过程需要消耗更多水资源。

sentences.english: And further resources are used as the cloth is dyed, made into clothing and transported to retail for sale.

sentences.english: Secondly, the fast-fashion industry is under pressure to put the latest trending items on shelves fast, which can lead to workers being exploited and forced to labour in poor working conditions.
sentences.chinese: 其次，快时尚行业面临着快速将最新潮流单品上架的压力，这可能导致工人遭受剥削，被迫在恶劣的工作环境中劳作。

sentences.english: In countries such as Bangladesh, Ethiopia and the Philippines, workers are paid wages that are insufficient to live on.
sentences.chinese: 在孟加拉国、埃塞俄比亚和菲律宾等国家，工人的工资难以维持基本生活。

sentences.chinese: 那么，英国可以采取哪些措施来减少衣物浪费呢？

sentences.english: The EAC has recommended eighteen improvements to the UK government, from increasing tax on purchases to fund recycling centres to introducing more sewing lessons in schools, encouraging a make do and mend attitude when things become threadbare.

sentences.english: What can we do?
sentences.chinese: 我们个人又能做些什么呢？

sentences.english: Shop “second-hand and vintage,” recommends Tolly Gregory, an ethical fashion blogger.
sentences.chinese: 环保时尚博主托莉·格雷戈里建议大家“购买二手和复古衣物”。

sentences.english: Kristabel Plummer, a London-based fashion blogger, who spoke to the BBC, also recommends “looking for quality” and “longevity”.
sentences.chinese: 伦敦时尚博主克里斯塔贝尔·普拉默在接受英国广播公司采访时也建议，要“注重服装质量”和“耐用性”。

sentences.english: So keep an eye out for durable, resilient, hardy apparel that resists wear and tear.
sentences.chinese: 因此，我们应该留意那些结实耐穿、不易磨损的衣物。

title: The hotel of mum and dad
paragraphs: "There's no place like home" This English saying has much truth in it: the best place to be is surrounded by our treasured possessions and our loved ones and with a roof over our head. And for many young adults, it's the only affordable place to stay; somewhere where they can receive first-class service from mum and dad. But this comes at a price!

In some countries, it's quite traditional for people in their late teens and early 20s to live at home with their parents, but in other places, flying the nest to start their own independent life is very desirable. There is no nagging, and you can come and go as you wish. But there's been a growing trend, in the UK at least, for young people to return home to live - or not to leave home at all. According to the UK's Office for National Statistics, about a quarter of young adults aged 20-34 live at home, and that figure has been growing.

A survey by a price comparison website found that 18% of adult children in the UK said they were moving back home because of debt, compared with 8% last year. More young people had lost their jobs, and others couldn't afford their rent compared with the previous year. So, it's easy to see why they're increasingly becoming home birds.

The BBC's Lucy Hooker explains that many returning adult children enjoy home comforts. These include cooked meals, a full fridge and cleaning, as well as their bills being covered by what is commonly called "the hotel of mum and dad". But for the "hoteliers", that's mum and dad, the survey found the average cost to them has gone up sharply, and that they are sacrificing luxuries and holidays to look after their "big kids". Emma Craig from Moneysupermarket says "they're trying to look after their children more. If your child comes home and you see them struggling financially, you feel more awkward asking them for rent or to contribute. It tugs on your heartstrings more."

With parents splashing out around £1,886 on takeaway food, buying new furniture and upgrading their Wi-Fi for the benefit of their offspring, it's easy for the returning children to put their feet up and make themselves at home. That's before they learn a home truth – that one day it might be their own kids who'll be checking into the hotel of mum and dad!

vocabulary.entry: treasured possession /ˈtreʒəd pəˈzeʃn/ 珍爱的物品
vocabulary.example: The old watch is one of my most treasured possessions.
vocabulary.translation: 这块旧手表是我最珍爱的物品之一。

vocabulary.entry: a roof over one's head /ə ruːf ˈəʊvə wʌnz hed/ 一处栖身之所；遮风挡雨的家
vocabulary.example: After losing his job, he struggled to keep a roof over his head.
vocabulary.translation: 失业后，他好不容易才维持住一处栖身之所。

vocabulary.entry: affordable /əˈfɔːdəbl/ adj. 负担得起的
vocabulary.example: The hotel offers affordable accommodation near the city centre.
vocabulary.translation: 这家酒店在市中心附近提供价格实惠的住宿。

vocabulary.entry: late teens /leɪt tiːnz/ 十八九岁
vocabulary.example: She started working part-time in her late teens.
vocabulary.translation: 她十八九岁时开始做兼职。

vocabulary.entry: fly the nest /flaɪ ðə nest/ 离家独立生活
vocabulary.example: Most young people fly the nest when they go to college.
vocabulary.translation: 大多数年轻人上大学时都会离家独立生活。

vocabulary.entry: nag /næɡ/ v. 唠叨；不停地抱怨
vocabulary.example: My mum always nags me about cleaning my room.
vocabulary.translation: 我妈妈总是唠叨我，让我打扫房间。

vocabulary.entry: growing trend /ˈɡrəʊɪŋ trend/ 日益明显的趋势
vocabulary.example: There is a growing trend towards online shopping among the elderly.
vocabulary.translation: 老年人网购的趋势越来越明显。

vocabulary.entry: home bird /həʊm bɜːd/ 恋家的人

sentences.english: In some countries, it's quite traditional for people in their late teens and early 20s to live at home with their parents, but in other places, flying the nest to start their own independent life is very desirable.

sentences.english: The BBC's Lucy Hooker explains that many returning adult children enjoy home comforts.
sentences.chinese: 英国广播公司的露西·胡克解释道，许多搬回家住的成年子女，都很享受家里的舒适便利。

sentences.english: These include cooked meals, a full fridge and cleaning, as well as their bills being covered by what is commonly called "the hotel of mum and dad".

sentences.english: But for the "hoteliers", that's mum and dad, the survey found the average cost to them has gone up sharply, and that they are sacrificing luxuries and holidays to look after their "big kids".

sentences.english: Emma Craig from Moneysupermarket says "they're trying to look after their children more.

title: Think positive!
paragraphs: How are you feeling today? If your head’s in a spin because you’ve had a bad night's sleep, or you’re hungover, or maybe you’ve just got too much to do, the chances are you’re not in the best of moods. If everything seems like an effort and you have a negative attitude, the last thing you want to be told it to ‘be positive!’ But having this mindset could have more benefits than you think.

Of course, developing a positive attitude is easier said than done – it doesn’t come naturally to everyone. When you’re feeling down in the dumps, it is hard to be optimistic. But a study in the US has found that people who are optimists are more likely to live longer than those who have a more negative approach to life. It revealed the likelihood of positive people living to the age of 85 or more to be higher. So, maybe the thought of a longer life might encourage you to have a more hopeful outlook on life.

The study concluded that optimists may find it easier to control emotions and get less stressed. And as stress impacts on the immune system, it’s possible that optimists cope better with infections. Professor Lewina Lee from Boston University School of Medicine, who worked on the study, told the BBC that: "Our findings speak to the possibility that raising levels of optimism may promote longevity and healthy ageing." And she advises that pessimists could benefit from doing things like imagining a future where everything turns out well.

But if you’re a ‘glass half empty’ type of person, could seeing the world through rose-tinted glasses work for you? Accepting that we all have problems and that we’re not all the same helps us to get a grip on our emotions. Some people say it’s best to celebrate the positives and not dwell on the negative parts of our lives.

People have being giving the BBC their personal advice on keeping a healthy and positive approach to life: Vicki Siska says "Music feeds my soul, a sense of humour keeps things in perspective, and I have good friends who love and care for me." And Pippa Kennedy says "being grateful for what you have - and lots of chocolate - helps!" The saying goes that ‘a healthy body leads a healthy mind’ which is probably why other people have recommended doing yoga and meditation as well as staying fit and healthy to help maintain a positive outlook on life.

title: The tipping taboo
paragraphs: It’s nice to go out for a meal at a restaurant. But what makes it extra special – apart from the food - is to receive attentive service from the staff. What can leave a bad taste in your mouth, though, is to be handed the bill and see that a service charge has been added. You’re faced with the dilemma of deciding to pay it, and whether you should add a tip on top.

Putting your hand in your pocket to reward good service is a personal choice, but it also depends on where you are in the world. What is the norm in one city is not necessarily the norm in another. In some places a tip is expected; but in others, good service should be expected and ought to be included in the price.

Adding an optional service charge to your bill certainly makes paying a tip less awkward because there’s no need to calculate the amount. But even though it’s not compulsory, you sometimes feel obliged to pay it. In the UK, where people tend to be too polite to complain, they might pay the service charge despite quietly complaining that the service they received was not up to scratch!

Choosing your own amount to tip may seem fairer, but should you pay it in cash or add it on to a credit card payment? And who will be the recipient? If we are to pay extra, we want to know it goes to the person who deserves it and that it’s not used as an alternative to paying someone a proper wage. In the UK in 2009, the law was changed after an outcry over staff being paid under the minimum wage and then topping up their wages with money they had earned in tips.

However, in the US it’s still customary to leave a gratuity because tips often make up a substantial part of a server’s income. Restaurant owner William Beckett told the BBC that in New York, for example, “There’s a tacit pressure to tip. But theoretically you (could) just stand up and walk out. You don’t. Everybody tips 20%.”

Maybe we should follow Japan’s approach, where tipping under any circumstance may seem rude because good service is standard and expected. Elsewhere, there are calls for restaurants to replace the tipping system with a so-called 'hospitality-included' charge – a single payment which covers both the meal and the service. This basically means, don’t tip - the price you see on the menu reflects the full cost of dining. That might make receiving the final bill easier to swallow!

title: The vegan fast food trend
paragraphs: There are around 600,000 vegans in the UK, according to The Vegan Society. That's just over 1% of the population – an amount expected to increase to 25% by 2025. And if there's one type of food that Brits love, it's fast food. True, it's not the most nutritious, but there's nothing quite like the crunch of crispy chips, or that first big bite into a juicy hamburger. People in the UK love junk food so much that there was a 34% increase in the number of fast food outlets from 2010 to 2018, according to the Office for National Statistics. It's no surprise, then, that vegan fast food is also on the rise.

Vegan fast food has become big business. At Just Eat, an online food delivery company, vegan orders more than doubled in 2018, a spokesperson told the BBC. Greggs, a chain of high-street bakeries, named its vegan sausage roll the 'fastest-selling product in six years'. And big franchises such as McDonald's and KFC have announced meat-free chicken nuggets to come in the future.

What's driving this popularity? Katrina Fox, founder of Vegan Business Media, believes it's the result of social media and the breaking down of stereotypes. "Vegan food is no longer seen as a bit of lettuce and lentils – you can eat pretty much anything," she told the BBC. It's also claimed that there are health benefits. John Marulanda, owner of Mooshies - a vegan burger bar in London – wants to implement "a change to a healthy version of fast food." Something, he claims, that comes as a result of the inherent nutritional value of the ingredients they use.

But, is vegan fast food actually healthy? Azmina Govindji of the British Dietetic Association says "not to assume" that is the case. "It's fine if those products have got vitamin B12, iodine or calcium added to them… but they can still be fried, it can still have lots of creamy, fatty sauces and lots of salt."

Given the current growth in orders, the trend for vegan fast food isn't likely to disappear any time soon. Health-wise, it may not be any more nourishing than regular fast food, but for many, the lack of animal suffering involved in the process is a big plus.

sentences.chinese: 但素食快餐真的健康吗？

sentences.english: Azmina Govindji of the British Dietetic Association says "not to assume" that is the case.
sentences.chinese: 英国饮食协会的阿兹米娜·戈文德吉表示，“不能想当然地”认为事实就是如此。

sentences.english: "It's fine if those products have got vitamin B12, iodine or calcium added to them… but they can still be fried, it can still have lots of creamy, fatty sauces and lots of salt."
sentences.chinese: “如果这些产品添加了维生素B12、碘或钙，那当然是好事……但它们仍可能经过油炸，可能含有大量奶油状高脂酱料，且含盐量不低。”

sentences.english: Given the current growth in orders, the trend for vegan fast food isn't likely to disappear any time soon.
sentences.chinese: 从目前订单的增长趋势来看，素食快餐的热潮短期内不太可能消退。

sentences.english: Health-wise, it may not be any more nourishing than regular fast food, but for many, the lack of animal suffering involved in the process is a big plus.
sentences.chinese: 就健康而言，它或许并不比普通快餐更具营养价值，但对许多人来说，生产过程中不涉及动物受苦，这便是一大优势。

title: The future of Britain's high streets
titleChinese: 英国传统购物街的未来
paragraphs: Do you like shopping? For shopaholics in the UK, the place to head to used to be the ‘high street’. This location refers to the streets in the centre of a town where businesses and popular branches of retail chains could be found. It was the place where you could find familiar fashion brands and essential everyday items. But change in our shopping habits has taken its toll on the British high street.

News about shops losing money and shutting is now common. Some city-centre department stores have closed and even long-established retailers such as Marks and Spencer have reported profit slumps. According to the accountancy firm Pricewaterhouse Coopers and the Local Data Company, a record 2,481 shops disappeared from UK high streets last year - up by 40%. Even some large warehouse-style stores in out-of-town retail parks, have gone bust and shut up shop.

As the BBC’s Emma Simpson writes, things have become a lot harder for traditional retailers in recent years. They have faced rising costs from wages, business rates and the requirement to introduce Europe’s new data law. But the biggest threat has come from online shopping. She says “Consumers now spend one in every five pounds online - and if businesses are seeing 20% fewer sales on the shop floor, as well as their fixed costs rising, then profit margins will be squeezed.”

While some of us like to window shop – browsing for things to buy, only to purchase them online at a discount - the fact is that, overall, shoppers are making fewer visits to high streets. Eventually, town centres could become like ghost towns. If people aren’t out and about shopping, they won’t use other services, like cafes, restaurants and cinemas. It also results in job losses. The British Retail Consortium has already warned that 900,000 UK retail jobs could be lost by 2025. The high street has also suffered from the advent of big shopping malls, which offer a retail experience under one roof, with free parking, away from the bad weather!

Meanwhile, back on the high street, some shops still exist. Analysts have said it’s those that have moved away from traditional retailing that are surviving. These include beauty salons, nail bars and independent coffee shops – but are these kinds of shops enough to keep the British high street open for business?
