title: Sustainable fabrics of the future
titleChinese: 既环保又耐用的未来服装面料
paragraphs: Choosing what to wear can be a tricky problem, especially if you’re a fashion victim. Trying to keep up with the latest styles involves regular visits to the shops and sometimes forking out for expensive designer clothes. But when the fashion changes, these clothes languish in the back of cupboards gathering dust, or just get thrown away.

There are many stores that now offer cheap ‘fast fashion’ – low-price items that imitate the styles of more expensive designer brands. Environmentalists are angered by the amount of energy involved in making these clothes and that many of them are made from non-recyclable materials. This means that items are just incinerated or go into landfill.

Writing about this for the BBC, Eleanor Lawrie says that people in the UK are the worst in Europe for doing this - with a million tonnes of unwanted textiles a year being discarded. And she says “on top of often poor labour conditions for garment workers, the fashion industry is responsible for 20% of the world's waste water, and 10% of carbon emissions.”

This is something the fashion industry is becoming more aware of and has led to a new crop of biomaterials that replace wasteful textiles like cotton and leather. Examples include Piñatex, a leather-like substance made from discarded pineapple leaves. It's been used in collections by Hugo Boss and H&M. And there’s mycelium, the root structure of mushrooms, that’s being used to create food, packaging and textiles.

Cotton is a very resource-intense crop to grow. Eleanor Lawrie says “about 15,000 litres of water [are] required to make one pair of jeans.” So, buying organic cotton is a better choice. And there is also Tencel, also known as Lyocell, a natural product that's now growing in popularity. It's made by extracting cellulose fibre from trees; its manufacture is thought to use 95% less water than cotton processing.

But creating sustainable textiles is only part of the battle – buying ethically, buying second hand and buying fewer clothes are the obvious environmentally friendly choices. Dr Richard Blackburn from Leeds School of Design told the BBC that “I don't think you should consider buying any item of clothing unless you commit to 30 wears. Unless you can do that you're not even starting to be sustainable.”

sentences.english: Writing about this for the BBC, Eleanor Lawrie says that people in the UK are the worst in Europe for doing this - with a million tonnes of unwanted textiles a year being discarded.

sentences.english: And she says “on top of often poor labour conditions for garment workers, the fashion industry is responsible for 20% of the world's waste water, and 10% of carbon emissions.”
sentences.chinese: 她还说：“除了服装工人往往面临恶劣的劳动条件外，时尚产业还造成了全球20%的废水排放和10%的碳排放。”

sentences.english: This is something the fashion industry is becoming more aware of and has led to a new crop of biomaterials that replace wasteful textiles like cotton and leather.
sentences.chinese: 时尚产业逐渐意识到这一问题，这也催生了一批新型生物材料，以替代棉花和皮革等耗资源的纺织品。

sentences.english: Examples include Piñatex, a leather-like substance made from discarded pineapple leaves. It's been used in collections by Hugo Boss and H&M.
sentences.chinese: 例如，Piñatex（菠萝皮皮革）是一种由废弃菠萝叶制成的类皮革材料，已被雨果博斯（Hugo Boss）和H&M用于服装系列中。

sentences.english: And there’s mycelium, the root structure of mushrooms, that’s being used to create food, packaging and textiles.
sentences.chinese: 还有菌丝体（蘑菇的根系结构），目前正被用于生产食品、包装和纺织品。

sentences.english: Cotton is a very resource-intense crop to grow.
sentences.chinese: 棉花是一种种植过程消耗资源极高的作物。

sentences.english: So, buying organic cotton is a better choice.

sentences.english: And there is also Tencel, also known as Lyocell, a natural product that's now growing in popularity.
sentences.chinese: 此外还有天丝（Tencel，也称为莱赛尔纤维），这是一种天然产品，如今正越来越受欢迎。

sentences.english: It's made by extracting cellulose fibre from trees; its manufacture is thought to use 95% less water than cotton processing.
sentences.chinese: 它通过从树木中提取纤维素纤维制成，其生产过程消耗的水量据信比棉花加工少95%。

sentences.english: But creating sustainable textiles is only part of the battle – buying ethically, buying second hand and buying fewer clothes are the obvious environmentally friendly choices.
sentences.chinese: 但制造可持续纺织品只是这场战役的一部分——理性消费（关注环保及劳工权益）、购买二手衣物以及减少购衣数量，才是显而易见的环保选择。

title: Using technology to keep employees happy
paragraphs: Going to work can be a slog, especially if your job is full of tedious tasks and pointless meetings. Obviously, work is necessary to earn an income, and if you get good job satisfaction it’s a bonus! But what can make it more worthwhile are the extra perks that your employer offers you as a reward for your loyalty and commitment.

Employee benefits are commonplace these days. Traditionally, these have included a good pension and extra days off work. But when a job used to be for life, there wasn’t much incentive to try and keep staff. Now millennials look to leave their jobs within the first two years, and when they are seeking a position, they want to know the benefits they’ll get on top of their pay. These include half-price cinema tickets, cycle to work schemes and gym passes.

But these perks come at a cost to an employer, and now technology is being used to discover if and when they offer value for money. Writing for the BBC, Jessica Bown says “Emerging technologies such as data analytics, chatbots, and wearables can help employers know which benefits resonate with employees.” The idea is to avoid wasting money on things that don’t get used and enable a company to tailor what it can offer to attract and retain the right staff.

As an example, at merchant bank, Close Brothers, AI has been used to develop chatbots that can help employees to find information on subjects ranging from mental health to saving for retirement at any time. And Microsoft has developed software to help businesses track their employee’s wellbeing needs. Anna Rasmussen, founder of Open Blend, told the BBC “It shows companies what their employees need to stay motivated and reach their full potential in real-time.” Insurance company Vitality offer wearable technology to track employees’ movements. Staff can earn ‘rewards’ by having their activity tracked. A study found that by measuring participant’s performance, they did the equivalent of 4.8 extra days of activity per month.

It seems that if used in the right way, technology can provide greater engagement between an employee and the company. That can lead to a happier, healthier and committed work force. But human resources experts warn against relying solely on tech for deciding on employee benefits provision. Greater understanding of new technology and how it’s used is needed, they say.

title: Can playing video games get you a better job
titleChinese: 玩电游能找到好工作吗？
paragraphs: Do you enjoy playing computer games? They can be thrilling, especially when you’re competing against others. They involve lots of skill, and offer a chance to switch off from the pressures of real life. But imagine if your gaming talents could actually be put to use in the real world? Well, now businesses are waking up to the skills gamers can bring to the workplace.

As an example, the BBC spoke to trainee surgeon Saied Froghi. He played video games like Age of Empires and Halo in his spare time when he was at medical school. But this relaxing pastime wasn’t distracting him from his studies - he thinks his time in front of a screen actually helped his surgery skills. He claims it helped him with his concentration, and he compares some of the skills used in keyhole surgery with using a games console. He says “Your hands know where the buttons are and how to rotate the instrument.”

Certainly, operating gaming controls help to develop good hand-eye coordination, but there are other abilities you can learn which can be applied to real-life work situations. Start-up company Game Academy told the BBC’s David Molloy that some games involve strategy and resource management, which are good skills for management. It analyses gamers' habits from their online gaming profile and offers courses in valuable skills that reflect their aptitudes. These are skills that can be developed, and if carefully reworded, can be added to CVs.

Employers might still need convincing that gamers are not just teenagers wasting their time in their bedrooms without thinking about their career prospects. But business consultant Mia Bennett told the BBC that gaming can help skills like "decision-making, the ability to anticipate and scenario planning… It also helps with meta-skills - learning how to learn, experimentation, and creative thinking."

You might think that the idea of gaming developing transferable skills is like the games themselves – pure fantasy – and a gamer doesn’t want to associate the fun and escapism it provides with work. It certainly doesn’t guarantee you a good job, and you need to be an accomplished gamer for your skills to shine. But if so much time is being spent gripped by the challenge of Portal or the strategy of Civilization, why not put those talents to good use?

title: The podcast boom
paragraphs: Do you prefer to watch TV or listen to the radio? There was a time when some people thought moving pictures beamed live into our houses would spell the end of tuning in to the radio for entertainment and information. But radio survived and flourished. And now, despite the growth in sophisticated smartphones offering high-definition pictures, the popularity of podcasts is booming.

Perhaps the growth in podcasting is not surprising – it offers a digital audio file that can be downloaded and stored for listening at any time. It can also be streamed from the internet and played on a computer or MP3 player. And it’s not just broadcasters, like the BBC, who are producing podcasts: now commercial broadcasters, individuals and companies with no connection to broadcasting are making them. In fact, anyone with something to say, and a few pounds to spend on the equipment, can get involved.

But where did this trend for making portable audio programmes begin? Journalist Ben Hammersley told the BBC that “two changes transformed the market – one cultural and one technical.” Apple launched the iPhone podcast app, recording and editing equipment became cheaper, and 4G mobile phone connections and Wi-Fi became widespread. Technological development has driven many changes in our media consumption habits. But however good the tech may be, there still needs to be something worth watching or listening to. The BBC’s Jamie Robertson writes that for podcasts, Serial - a piece of non-fiction investigative journalism – captured people’s imagination. It was a piece of high-quality audio with a gripping story. To date, the first and second seasons of the show have had more than 340 million downloads. Advertisers soon realised the money-making potential of this and other successful podcasts.

Now there are podcasts about anything and everything - even the educational content that BBC Learning English offers! And these aural treats are available on a wide range of platforms. Audiences are very specific, which can help advertisers target what they want to promote. And if there isn’t a podcast to suit your interests, you can now easily make and distribute them - and become your very own broadcaster.

title: Slow walking and ageing
paragraphs: Getting old might not be something that’s yet to cross your mind. But ageing is inevitably going to get the better of us one day, so it’s something I’m sure we’d all like control. It would be great to have a long, healthy and happy life, and that’s why scientists are constantly seeking out evidence that will show us what we need to do to achieve longevity.

We all know that regular exercise is good for us. In recent years we’ve been told to aim to walk 10,000 steps a day to remain healthy, although other advice to do three brisk 10-minute walks a day is thought to be even more effective. But the latest piece of research might put a spring in your step if you’re someone who walks at a fast pace. That’s because, according to scientists, the speed at which people walk in their 40s is a sign of how much their brains, as well as their bodies, are ageing.

The BBC’s Philippa Roxby writes that tests on 1,000 people from New Zealand born in the 1970s found that slower walkers tended to show signs of "accelerated ageing". Their lungs, teeth and immune systems were in worse shape than those who walked faster. And to add insult to injury, the study found not only did slower walkers' bodies age more quickly, their faces looked older and they had smaller brains. Professor Terrie E Moffitt, lead author of the study, told the BBC: "[it] found that a slow walk is a problem sign decades before old age."

This might be seen as a wake-up call for people with a slower gait who might feel it’s time to work out and get fitter. But it might be too late; researchers writing in JAMA Network Open say they were able to predict the walking speed of 45-year-olds using the results of intelligence, language and motor skills tests from when they were aged three. They also suggest that even in early life, there are signs showing which people will go on to have a healthier life.

So, what’s the point of knowing that a slower walking pace might mean a smaller brain? Well, researchers say measuring walking speed at a younger age, and understanding what this might mean, could be a way of testing treatments to slow human ageing. This might help us make lifestyle changes while we’re still young and healthy. Any steps we can take to prolong a good mental and physical state is a no brainer!

sentences.english: Getting old might not be something that’s yet to cross your mind.

sentences.english: It would be great to have a long, healthy and happy life, and that’s why scientists are constantly seeking out evidence that will show us what we need to do to achieve longevity.
sentences.chinese: 拥有漫长、健康且幸福的人生是件美好的事，这也是科学家们不断寻找证据，想要告诉我们如何才能实现长寿的原因。

sentences.english: That’s because, according to scientists, the speed at which people walk in their 40s is a sign of how much their brains, as well as their bodies, are ageing.
sentences.chinese: 这是因为科学家们发现，人们在40多岁时的步行速度，能反映出他们的大脑和身体的衰老程度。

sentences.english: The BBC’s Philippa Roxby writes that tests on 1,000 people from New Zealand born in the 1970s found that slower walkers tended to show signs of "accelerated ageing".
sentences.chinese: 英国广播公司的菲利帕·罗克斯比写道，对1000名出生于20世纪70年代的新西兰人进行的测试发现，走路较慢的人往往表现出“加速衰老”的迹象。

sentences.english: Their lungs, teeth and immune systems were in worse shape than those who walked faster.
sentences.chinese: 他们的肺部、牙齿和免疫系统状况都比走路较快的人更差。

sentences.english: And to add insult to injury, the study found not only did slower walkers' bodies age more quickly, their faces looked older and they had smaller brains.
sentences.chinese: 更糟糕的是，研究还发现，走路慢的人不仅身体衰老得更快，面容看起来也更显老，大脑也更小。

sentences.english: Professor Terrie E Moffitt, lead author of the study, told the BBC: "[it] found that a slow walk is a problem sign decades before old age."
sentences.chinese: 该研究的主要作者特里·E·莫菲特教授向英国广播公司表示：“（研究）发现，走路慢是老年期到来前几十年就会出现的问题信号。”

sentences.english: This might be seen as a wake-up call for people with a slower gait who might feel it’s time to work out and get fitter.
sentences.chinese: 这或许会给走路缓慢的人敲响警钟，让他们意识到是时候锻炼身体、增强体质了。

sentences.english: But it might be too late; researchers writing in JAMA Network Open say they were able to predict the walking speed of 45-year-olds using the results of intelligence, language and motor skills tests from when they were aged three.
sentences.chinese: 但也许为时已晚：发表在《美国医学会网络开放期刊》上的研究称，研究人员通过分析人们三岁时的智力、语言和运动技能测试结果，就能预测他们45岁时的步行速度。

sentences.english: They also suggest that even in early life, there are signs showing which people will go on to have a healthier life.
sentences.chinese: 研究人员还表示，即使在生命早期，就有迹象能表明哪些人未来会拥有更健康的人生。

sentences.english: So, what’s the point of knowing that a slower walking pace might mean a smaller brain?
sentences.chinese: 那么，知道走路速度慢可能意味着大脑体积小，又有什么意义呢？

sentences.english: Well, researchers say measuring walking speed at a younger age, and understanding what this might mean, could be a way of testing treatments to slow human ageing.
sentences.chinese: 研究人员表示，在年轻时测量步行速度，并了解其背后的含义，可能会成为测试延缓人类衰老疗法的一种方式。

sentences.english: This might help us make lifestyle changes while we’re still young and healthy.
sentences.chinese: 这有助于我们在年轻健康的时候就做出生活方式上的改变。

sentences.english: Any steps we can take to prolong a good mental and physical state is a no brainer!

title: Make-up's little secret
paragraphs: Have you ever gone out without putting your face on? Whether it's a dash of foundation or a full application of lipstick, blusher or mascara, many would consider make-up essential before being seen. According to a survey by Fragrance Direct, a leading UK beauty retailer, the average UK woman uses twelve beauty products in their beauty regime daily – that's approximately £500 spent annually. But behind the monetary cost lies another, and it's one that many consumers may not know about.

70% of cosmetics are manufactured using palm oil – a substance which is controversial, and, according to many, environmentally damaging. Between 1990 and 2008, oil palm tree plantations were responsible for the deforestation of around 8% of the world's forests, according to the BBC. This leads to a loss of biodiversity and habitat for wildlife – particularly those already under threat, such as the orangutan. And demand for the crop is increasing.

To further complicate things, we can't simply ban it or stop using it. It's the most widely used vegetable oil on the planet and responsible for an industry worth more than $40 billion. Stopping its production would ruin many people's livelihoods worldwide. Worse, alternative vegetable oils, such as rapeseed, coconut or sunflower, would require up to ten times as much land to produce the same amount. This would only exacerbate the issue.

There is hope, though, of sustainable palm oil based on a global standard set by the Round Table on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO) – a group of growers, retailers, NGOs and manufacturers. To meet their standards, a company must not clear any primary forest, treat workers fairly, and create wildlife zones, among other things. However, many critics say that these rules are not strict enough. According to a report by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature, there is limited evidence of effective conservation as a result.

That said, in 2016, 75% of the total palm oil imports to the UK were sustainable, according to the BBC. Many retailers and leading brands use it, but as a consumer, knowing which is which can be difficult. The RSPO has a logo, but it rarely gets printed on the cosmetic label. The best we can do for now is check the ingredients carefully and do some research.

title: What’s a narcissist like
paragraphs: It takes all sorts to make a world – so some say. Nobody is the same, and our different personalities and character traits make us what we are. Wouldn’t it be boring if we were all the same? But if someone doesn’t behave or think like you, it can be frustrating. And there’s one personality type that can be very difficult to deal with - narcissism.

Narcissists consider themselves the most important person. They’re only interested in their own life, without a care in the world about the people around them. Their lack of empathy makes them come across as arrogant and self-important. If you know someone like this, their narcissistic attitudes might irritate you. But you might find it even more irritating to know that, according to new research, they are likely to be happier than other people.

An ongoing study of narcissism by researchers at Queen's University Belfast has found such people might infuriate others but are less likely to be stressed or depressed. Writing about the research, the BBC’s Sean Coughlan says “They might have trampled over others and left a trail of emotional damage around them - but narcissists also seem to be insulated against feeling bad about themselves.” And their heightened sense of self-importance appears to give them "protective" qualities.

Researchers have been trying to understand why narcissism appears to be more prevalent in areas such as politics, social media and celebrity culture and why narcissists' shameless, over-confident attitude seems to be rewarded rather than penalised. It does seem that they have the best of all worlds, which is not great news for shrinking violets. And there’s more bad news for those who are shy and retiring: previous research by Queen’s University has also found that a ‘mental toughness’ helps narcissists succeed at work and in their social lives because they can overcome rejection and disappointment. And other tests have found that narcissistic students do better in exams, not because they are more clever, but because of their confidence and assertiveness.

But psychologist Dr Kostas Papageorgiou from the research team argues that these personality traits should not be seen as "either good or bad" but as "products of evolution" and "expressions of human nature". So, at the end of the day, we are what we are, and that’s just something we can’t change.

title: Happy or sad What type of music do you like
titleChinese: 你喜欢悲伤还是快乐的音乐？
paragraphs: What would life be like without music? Songs and tunes fill our lives, affecting our emotions, bringing back memories and sometimes making us dance. There is a song for everyone and for every occasion, but it seems that it’s sad music that moves us most.

Sad music certainly does its job in making us depressed, emotional, and causing us to sob – it’s something we might listen to after a break-up, for example. And a recent study has shown why some people are hooked on sad music. Professor David Huron from Ohio State University conducted the research and looked at the difference between people who love to listen to sad music and those who can’t stand it.

He told the BBC radio programme The Why Factor that it comes down to a natural hormone called prolactin. He says: “as you might have guessed from the name, it's associated with ‘lactation’ from breast-feeding. When people cry, they also release prolactin. And, there are circumstances in which prolactin seems to have this comforting effect.” It seems that people who like sad music are maybe getting too much prolactin, or more than is normal, and when they hear sad, downbeat music, it gives them a good feeling. But if prolactin isn’t released, or there isn’t enough of it, some people find the sad sounds don’t help to cheer them up.

Previous research by Durham University has also suggested that listening to sad music can trigger pain and sadness; but it can also provide comfort and even enjoyment. A high number of people they surveyed were cheered up by listening to supposedly sad songs. Though the feeling may not be exactly the same as happiness, it may be the ability to cope with the sadness that gives the feeling of comfort.

So, reacting to sad music on the radio may have nothing to do with the melancholic sound of a string quartet or a singer who’s got the blues, but rather a natural chemical reaction taking place in our bodies. Maybe that explanation is music to your ears if you're wondering why you’ve been listening to Adele on repeat!

title: Weird job interviews
paragraphs: Finding a new job isn’t always easy. You search for a suitable vacancy, send in an application form and if that goes well, you might be invited for an interview. For some, this is when the panic sets in – you’re going to be faced by a panel of strangers who’ll fire difficult questions at you, and you’ll have to actually prove yourself. But how would you feel if, instead of being asked why you want the job, you’re asked to stand up and dance?!

From the perspective of a company, it wants to hire the right person because they can make a big difference to the success of the organisation. It therefore needs to test a candidate in the most appropriate way to discover how suitable he or she may be. A good interview process should involve rigorous screening of job applicants and effective questions that every applicant gets asked. But that’s not always the case.

Alison Green is an author and creator of the workplace advice column 'Ask a Manager'. She told the BBC that some companies “give their interviewers little or no training and often leave them completely on their own when it comes to figuring out what to ask job candidates.” She mentions that some interviewers are too casual and some focus on building a good rapport and end up hiring the candidate they just ‘clicked with’, regardless of their skills and abilities.

An inexperienced interviewer may think it’s clever to ask ‘if you were an animal, what kind would you be?’ That has been asked, Alison Green says, but in reality this has no connection with the job. And there have been inappropriate requests, such as one job seeker being asked to show the interviewer the inside of her handbag to demonstrate how organised she was.

Talking of inappropriate, the BBC heard from a number of people who were surprised by the questions they were asked in an interview. Mature student Kevin Helton said that "the interviewer asked, 'you used to be in the Army, how many people have you killed?'”

But as Alison Green points out, while a candidate might feel at the mercy of an interviewer, they are able to question why they’re being asked something, and while the interviewer might be making judgements, the candidate can also make their own judgement and decide if this is really the career move they want to make!

vocabulary.translation: 随着截止日期的临近，团队中开始出现恐慌。

vocabulary.entry: panel /ˈpænl/ n. （面试）小组；评审团
vocabulary.example: The candidate faced a panel of three interviewers.
vocabulary.translation: 这位候选人面对的是一个由三名面试官组成的小组。

vocabulary.entry: fire questions /ˈfaɪə(r) ˈkwestʃənz/ 抛出问题；接连发问
vocabulary.example: The journalists fired questions at the politician during the press conference.
vocabulary.translation: 新闻发布会期间，记者们向这位政客接连发问。

vocabulary.entry: prove oneself /pruːv wʌnˈself/ 证明自己
vocabulary.example: She was determined to prove herself in her new role.
vocabulary.translation: 她决心在新岗位上证明自己。

vocabulary.entry: hire /ˈhaɪə(r)/ v. 聘用；雇用
vocabulary.example: The company plans to hire five new employees next month.
vocabulary.translation: 这家公司计划下个月聘用五名新员工。

vocabulary.entry: candidate /ˈkændɪdət/ n. 候选人；求职者
vocabulary.example: We have shortlisted ten candidates for the job.
vocabulary.translation: 我们已经筛选出十位该职位的候选人。

vocabulary.entry: rigorous screening /ˈrɪɡərəs ˈskriːnɪŋ/ 严格筛选
vocabulary.example: All applicants undergo rigorous screening before being invited for an interview.
vocabulary.translation: 所有申请人在收到面试邀请前都会经过严格筛选。

vocabulary.entry: rapport /rəˈpɔː(r)/ n. 融洽关系；默契
vocabulary.example: She quickly built a good rapport with her new colleagues.
vocabulary.translation: 她很快就和新同事建立了良好的融洽关系。

vocabulary.entry: click with /klɪk wɪð/ 与……一拍即合；合得来
vocabulary.example: I clicked with my new roommate from the first day we met.
vocabulary.translation: 我和新室友从第一天见面就一拍即合。

vocabulary.entry: inexperienced /ˌɪnɪkˈspɪəriənst/ adj. 缺乏经验的；新手的
vocabulary.example: The team is led by an inexperienced manager.
vocabulary.translation: 这个团队由一位缺乏经验的经理带领。

vocabulary.entry: have no connection with /hæv nəʊ kəˈnekʃn wɪð/ 与……毫无关联
vocabulary.example: His comment has no connection with the topic we’re discussing.
vocabulary.translation: 他的评论与我们正在讨论的话题毫无关联。

vocabulary.entry: inappropriate /ˌɪnəˈprəʊpriət/ adj. 不合适的；不合时宜的
vocabulary.example: It’s inappropriate to make jokes about such a serious matter.
vocabulary.translation: 对如此严肃的事情开玩笑是不合适的。

vocabulary.entry: demonstrate /ˈdemənstreɪt/ v. 证明；展示
vocabulary.example: She demonstrated her ability to solve problems quickly.
vocabulary.translation: 她展示了自己快速解决问题的能力。

vocabulary.entry: organised /ˈɔːɡənaɪzd/ adj. 有条理的；有组织的
vocabulary.example: He’s a very organised person and always keeps his desk tidy.
vocabulary.translation: 他是个非常有条理的人，总是把办公桌收拾得很整洁。

vocabulary.entry: mature student /məˈtʃʊə(r) ˈstjuːdənt/ 成年学生；大龄学生
vocabulary.example: The college offers special support for mature students returning to education.
vocabulary.translation: 这所大学为重返校园的成年学生提供特殊支持。

vocabulary.entry: at the mercy of /æt ðə ˈmɜːsi əv/ 受制于；受……支配
vocabulary.example: Without a car, we were at the mercy of public transport.
vocabulary.translation: 没有汽车，我们只能受制于公共交通。

vocabulary.entry: make judgements /meɪk ˈdʒʌdʒmənts/ 做出判断；下结论
vocabulary.example: We should not make judgements based on appearance alone.
vocabulary.translation: 我们不应该仅凭外表做出判断。

vocabulary.entry: career move /kəˈrɪə muːv/ 职业变动；职业举措
vocabulary.example: Taking this job was a bold career move for her.
vocabulary.translation: 接受这份工作对她来说是一次大胆的职业变动。

vocabulary.entry: figure out /ˈfɪɡə(r) aʊt/ 弄清楚；想出
vocabulary.example: I need to figure out how to solve this problem by tomorrow.
vocabulary.translation: 我需要在明天之前弄清楚如何解决这个问题。

sentences.english: Finding a new job isn’t always easy.
sentences.chinese: 找新工作并不总是一帆风顺的。

sentences.english: You search for a suitable vacancy, send in an application form and if that goes well, you might be invited for an interview.
sentences.chinese: 你要寻找合适的职位空缺，提交申请表，如果一切顺利，可能会收到面试邀请。

sentences.english: For some, this is when the panic sets in – you’re going to be faced by a panel of strangers who’ll fire difficult questions at you, and you’ll have to actually prove yourself.
sentences.chinese: 对有些人来说，这时恐慌就会袭来——你要面对一群陌生人组成的面试小组，他们会抛出刁钻的问题，而你必须实实在在地证明自己的能力。

sentences.english: But how would you feel if, instead of being asked why you want the job, you’re asked to stand up and dance?!
sentences.chinese: 但如果面试官不问你“为什么想要这份工作”，反而让你站起来跳舞，你会是什么感受？

sentences.english: From the perspective of a company, it wants to hire the right person because they can make a big difference to the success of the organisation.
sentences.chinese: 从公司的角度来看，它希望招聘到合适的人，因为这些人能对组织的成功产生重大影响。

sentences.english: It therefore needs to test a candidate in the most appropriate way to discover how suitable he or she may be.
sentences.chinese: 因此，公司需要以最恰当的方式测试候选人，以了解其是否胜任岗位。

sentences.english: A good interview process should involve rigorous screening of job applicants and effective questions that every applicant gets asked.
sentences.chinese: 一个完善的面试流程应包括对求职者的严格筛选，以及向每位求职者提出有效的问题。

sentences.english: But that’s not always the case.
sentences.chinese: 但实际情况并非总是如此。

sentences.english: Alison Green is an author and creator of the workplace advice column 'Ask a Manager'.
sentences.chinese: 艾莉森·格林是职场建议专栏《咨询经理》（Ask a Manager）的作者和创始人。

sentences.english: She told the BBC that some companies “give their interviewers little or no training and often leave them completely on their own when it comes to figuring out what to ask job candidates.”
sentences.chinese: 她向英国广播公司表示，一些公司“给面试官的培训很少或根本没有，在决定该问求职者什么问题时，往往让他们完全自行决定”。

sentences.english: She mentions that some interviewers are too casual and some focus on building a good rapport and end up hiring the candidate they just ‘clicked with’, regardless of their skills and abilities.
sentences.chinese: 她提到，有些面试官过于随意，有些则专注于建立融洽的关系，最终聘用了那些与他们“合拍”的候选人，而忽视了其实际技能和能力。

sentences.english: An inexperienced interviewer may think it’s clever to ask ‘if you were an animal, what kind would you be?’
sentences.chinese: 缺乏经验的面试官可能会觉得问“如果你是一种动物，你会是什么动物？”很巧妙。

sentences.english: That has been asked, Alison Green says, but in reality this has no connection with the job.
sentences.chinese: 艾莉森·格林说，确实有人被问过这个问题，但实际上这与工作毫无关联。

sentences.english: And there have been inappropriate requests, such as one job seeker being asked to show the interviewer the inside of her handbag to demonstrate how organised she was.
sentences.chinese: 还有些不合时宜的要求，比如有求职者被要求向面试官展示手提包内部，以证明自己多么有条理。

sentences.english: Talking of inappropriate, the BBC heard from a number of people who were surprised by the questions they were asked in an interview.
sentences.chinese: 说到不合时宜，英国广播公司还收到了不少人的反馈，他们都对面试中被问到的问题感到惊讶。

sentences.english: Mature student Kevin Helton said that "the interviewer asked, 'you used to be in the Army, how many people have you killed?'”
sentences.chinese: 成年学生凯文·赫尔顿说：“面试官问我，‘你以前当过兵，杀过多少人？’”

sentences.english: But as Alison Green points out, while a candidate might feel at the mercy of an interviewer, they are able to question why they’re being asked something, and while the interviewer might be making judgements, the candidate can also make their own judgement and decide if this is really the career move they want to make!
sentences.chinese: 但正如艾莉森·格林所指出的，虽然候选人可能会觉得自己受制于面试官，但他们有权询问被问此类问题的原因。而且，面试官在做出判断的同时，候选人也可以自行判断，决定这是否真的是自己想要的职业变动！

title: Are all meetings necessary
titleChinese: 所有的会议都是必要的吗？
paragraphs: It’s time for another meeting! If you have a job, the chances are some of your working week will be taken up attending a few of them. You and your colleagues will gather together in a meeting room, be talked at for an hour and come out wondering what was the point of it? Of course, it is sometimes necessary to meet to discuss things, share information, voice your opinion and agree a way forward – but are there any other benefits?

Recent research has suggested that we attend more meetings than ever before – and that's more time listening and talking than actually doing our jobs. Professor Patrik Hall from the University of Malmo told the BBC that this is partly due to more “meetings-intense” roles such as managerial and strategy jobs. These require more meetings with teams and other stakeholders. But, he says, despite there being more of them, "few decisions are made".

It’s possible that it’s managers on a power trip who set up these meetings – a way of controlling staff, imposing new rules and regulations and asserting their authority. But as Professor Hall points out: "Many managers don't know what to do," and when they are "unsure of their role", they respond by generating more meetings. And to make matters worse, some meetings involve a pre or post-meeting which eats into even more of the working day.

But the researchers from the University of Malmo have found that a meeting can be seen as a form of ‘therapy’ – it doesn’t have to have an outcome and doesn’t have to be meaningless. So, if you’re just doodling or glancing at your smartphone as your boss drones on, it’s worth considering that a meeting can be an opportunity to demonstrate your talents, express frustration, question ideas and spend time bonding with your colleagues.

There are a few things to be considered if a meeting is to be a success: it needs an agenda that is adhered to plus an opportunity to discuss any other business, and it should be booked for a short period of time – otherwise the meeting will expand to fit the time that’s been allocated. And, as Professor Hall says, the “equality” of participants is important. But I think I just prefer the advice of Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, who urged colleagues to walk out of meetings as soon as it becomes obvious that they are not adding value. "It's not rude to leave," he explains. "It's rude to make someone stay and waste their time." Right, I’m off!

vocabulary.entry: take up /teɪk ʌp/ 占用（时间、空间）
vocabulary.example: Meetings take up a large part of my working day.
vocabulary.translation: 会议占用了我工作日的很大一部分时间。

vocabulary.entry: voice your opinion /vɔɪs jɔː(r) əˈpɪnjən/ 表达观点；发表意见
vocabulary.example: Don’t be afraid to voice your opinion during the discussion.
vocabulary.translation: 讨论时别害怕表达你的观点。

vocabulary.entry: agree a way forward /əˈɡriː ə weɪ ˈfɔːwəd/ 商定前进方向；达成行动共识
vocabulary.example: We need to agree a way forward before the project starts.
vocabulary.translation: 项目开始前，我们需要商定前进方向。

vocabulary.entry: meetings-intense /ˈmiːtɪŋz ɪnˈtens/ adj. 会议密集的
vocabulary.example: Managerial roles are often meetings-intense in large companies.
vocabulary.translation: 大公司的管理岗位通常是会议密集型的。

vocabulary.entry: managerial /ˌmænəˈdʒɪəriəl/ adj. 管理的；经理的
vocabulary.example: She has extensive managerial experience in the tech industry.
vocabulary.translation: 她在科技行业拥有丰富的管理经验。

vocabulary.entry: stakeholder /ˈsteɪkhəʊldə(r)/ n. 利益相关者
vocabulary.example: The company consulted all stakeholders before making the decision.
vocabulary.translation: 公司做决定前咨询了所有利益相关者。

vocabulary.entry: power trip /ˈpaʊə(r) trɪp/ 满足权力欲；权力炫耀
vocabulary.example: Some managers hold unnecessary meetings just for a power trip.
vocabulary.translation: 有些经理召开不必要的会议，只是为了满足权力欲。

vocabulary.entry: impose /ɪmˈpəʊz/ v. 推行；强制实施
vocabulary.example: The government imposed new rules on environmental protection.
vocabulary.translation: 政府推行了新的环保规定。

vocabulary.entry: assert one's authority /əˈsɜːt wʌnz ɔːˈθɒrəti/ 彰显权威；维护权力
vocabulary.example: The new director quickly asserted his authority by reorganizing the team.
vocabulary.translation: 新主管通过重组团队迅速彰显了自己的权威。

vocabulary.entry: generate /ˈdʒenəreɪt/ v. 产生；发起（此处指召开会议）
vocabulary.example: The team leader generates too many meetings that waste time.
vocabulary.translation: 团队领导召开了太多浪费时间的会议。

vocabulary.entry: eat into /iːt ˈɪntu/ 侵蚀；占用（时间、资源）
vocabulary.example: Unplanned tasks ate into our working hours this week.
vocabulary.translation: 本周临时任务占用了我们的工作时间。

vocabulary.entry: therapy /ˈθerəpi/ n. 疗愈；心理治疗
vocabulary.example: Some people find talking to colleagues in meetings a form of therapy.
vocabulary.translation: 有些人觉得在会议上和同事交流是一种心理疗愈。

vocabulary.entry: doodle /ˈduːdl/ v. 涂鸦；随意乱画
vocabulary.example: She doodled on her notebook while listening to the lecture.
vocabulary.translation: 她听讲座时在笔记本上涂鸦。

vocabulary.entry: drone on /drəʊn ɒn/ 喋喋不休；单调地说
vocabulary.example: The speaker droned on for hours without getting to the point.
vocabulary.translation: 演讲者喋喋不休地讲了几个小时，却没说到重点。

vocabulary.entry: demonstrate /ˈdemənstreɪt/ v. 展示；证明
vocabulary.example: He demonstrated his problem-solving skills during the meeting.
vocabulary.translation: 他在会议上展示了自己解决问题的能力。

vocabulary.entry: bond with /bɒnd wɪð/ 与……建立感情；增进联系
vocabulary.example: We bonded with our new colleagues during the team-building meeting.
vocabulary.translation: 我们在团建会议上与新同事建立了感情。

vocabulary.entry: agenda /əˈdʒendə/ n. 议程；议事日程
vocabulary.example: Could you send me the agenda for tomorrow's meeting?
vocabulary.translation: 你能把明天会议的议程发给我吗？

vocabulary.entry: adhere to /ədˈhɪə(r) tu/ 遵守；坚持
vocabulary.example: The team must adhere to the agenda to finish the meeting on time.
vocabulary.translation: 团队必须遵守议程，才能按时结束会议。

vocabulary.entry: allocate /ˈæləkeɪt/ v. 分配；分派（时间、资源等）
vocabulary.example: We allocated two hours for the meeting, but it lasted three.
vocabulary.translation: 我们给会议分配了两个小时，但它开了三个小时。

vocabulary.entry: equality /iˈkwɒləti/ n. 平等；均等
vocabulary.example: Equality of opportunity is important for effective team meetings.
vocabulary.translation: 机会均等对有效的团队会议很重要。

vocabulary.entry: add value /æd ˈvæljuː/ 增添价值；有意义
vocabulary.example: Only attend meetings where you can add value to the discussion.
vocabulary.translation: 只参加那些你能为讨论增添价值的会议。

vocabulary.entry: walk out /wɔːk aʊt/ 退出；离场
vocabulary.example: Several employees walked out of the meeting because they disagreed with the decision.
vocabulary.translation: 几名员工因为不同意这个决定，退出了会议。

sentences.english: It’s time for another meeting!
sentences.chinese: 又要开会了！

sentences.english: If you have a job, the chances are some of your working week will be taken up attending a few of them.
sentences.chinese: 如果你有工作，那么你一周的工作时间中，很可能会有一部分用来参加几次会议。

sentences.english: You and your colleagues will gather together in a meeting room, be talked at for an hour and come out wondering what was the point of it?
sentences.chinese: 你和同事们会聚集在会议室里，听人喋喋不休地讲一个小时，出来后却在想：这会议到底有什么意义？

sentences.english: Of course, it is sometimes necessary to meet to discuss things, share information, voice your opinion and agree a way forward – but are there any other benefits?
sentences.chinese: 当然，有时候开会是必要的——讨论事情、分享信息、表达观点、商定前进方向——但除此之外，还有其他好处吗？

sentences.english: Recent research has suggested that we attend more meetings than ever before – and that's more time listening and talking than actually doing our jobs.
sentences.chinese: 最近的研究表明，我们参加的会议比以往任何时候都多——而且花在听和说上的时间，比实际工作的时间还要多。

sentences.english: Professor Patrik Hall from the University of Malmo told the BBC that this is partly due to more “meetings-intense” roles such as managerial and strategy jobs.
sentences.chinese: 马尔默大学的帕特里克·霍尔教授向英国广播公司表示，部分原因是出现了更多“会议密集型”岗位，比如管理岗和战略岗。

sentences.english: These require more meetings with teams and other stakeholders.
sentences.chinese: 这些岗位需要与团队及其他利益相关者召开更多会议。

sentences.english: But, he says, despite there being more of them, "few decisions are made".
sentences.chinese: 但他说，尽管会议变多了，“却很少做出决策”。

sentences.english: It’s possible that it’s managers on a power trip who set up these meetings – a way of controlling staff, imposing new rules and regulations and asserting their authority.
sentences.chinese: 有可能是那些一心满足权力欲的经理们安排了这些会议——这是他们控制员工、推行新规章制度、彰显权威的一种方式。

sentences.english: But as Professor Hall points out: "Many managers don't know what to do," and when they are "unsure of their role", they respond by generating more meetings.
sentences.chinese: 但正如霍尔教授所指出的：“很多经理不知道该做什么”，当他们“对自己的角色感到不确定时”，就会通过召开更多会议来应对。

sentences.english: And to make matters worse, some meetings involve a pre or post-meeting which eats into even more of the working day.
sentences.chinese: 更糟糕的是，有些会议还会附带会前会或会后会，这进一步占用了工作日的时间。

sentences.english: But the researchers from the University of Malmo have found that a meeting can be seen as a form of ‘therapy’ – it doesn’t have to have an outcome and doesn’t have to be meaningless.
sentences.chinese: 但马尔默大学的研究人员发现，会议可以被视为一种“心理疗愈”——它不一定需要有结果，也不一定是毫无意义的。

sentences.english: So, if you’re just doodling or glancing at your smartphone as your boss drones on, it’s worth considering that a meeting can be an opportunity to demonstrate your talents, express frustration, question ideas and spend time bonding with your colleagues.
sentences.chinese: 所以，当你的老板喋喋不休时，如果你只是在涂鸦或翻看手机，不妨想一想：会议其实可以是一个展示才华、表达不满、质疑想法以及与同事建立感情的机会。

sentences.english: There are a few things to be considered if a meeting is to be a success: it needs an agenda that is adhered to plus an opportunity to discuss any other business, and it should be booked for a short period of time – otherwise the meeting will expand to fit the time that’s been allocated.
sentences.chinese: 要让会议取得成功，有几件事需要考虑：需要有一个严格遵守的议程，加上可以讨论其他事项的机会，而且会议时间应该预约得短一些——否则会议会自动拉长，填满分配给它的时间。

sentences.english: And, as Professor Hall says, the “equality” of participants is important.
sentences.chinese: 此外，正如霍尔教授所说，参会者之间的“平等性”也很重要。

sentences.english: But I think I just prefer the advice of Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, who urged colleagues to walk out of meetings as soon as it becomes obvious that they are not adding value.
sentences.chinese: 但我更倾向于特斯拉和SpaceX的首席执行官埃隆·马斯克的建议，他敦促同事们，一旦发现会议对自己没有价值，就立即离开。

sentences.english: "It's not rude to leave," he explains. "It's rude to make someone stay and waste their time."
sentences.chinese: “离开并不无礼，”他解释道，“让别人留下来浪费时间才是无礼的。”

sentences.english: Right, I’m off!
sentences.chinese: 好了，我要走了！

title: Tattoos good or bad
paragraphs: Do you have any tattoos? I don't. I've never been brave enough to go under the needle. But if you do have one, you are not alone. According to a report by Experian, the number of tattoo parlours in Britain increased by 173% between 2004 and 2014. Tattoos have always been controversial – personally and culturally. Some people love them and some hate them. So, are they good or bad?

These days, one in five people in the UK has some ink – whether it's a commemorative date, a sleeve or a full body suit. What's responsible for this rise in popularity? "You see a lot of celebrities getting tattooed," says Lee Clements of the British Tattoo Artist Association speaking on BBC radio. As a result, people want to copy them or it becomes a fashion thing – certain tattoos become a trend.

Employers have become more accepting of visible tats too. Last year, London's Metropolitan Police relaxed a ban on recruiting candidates with visible body art. And earlier this year, Air New Zealand said it would end a ban on body art to allow workers to express their individuality and cultural heritage.

That said, not all employers would agree. Grace, 28, told the BBC that she had been offered jobs in sales, which were then withdrawn when employers saw her hand tattoo. "It feels like having a tattoo is not socially acceptable," she says. "Having a tattoo does not amount to a protected characteristic," remarks Susan Harris, legal director at the GMB union, a UK trade union. This means a person can be dismissed for having one if it breaches the employer's dress code – except on religious grounds.

And let's not forget the risk of infection. At present anyone in the UK can set up a parlour and offer procedures without proper training, a report from the Royal Society for Public Health says. They note that just under 20% of those tattooed experience negative side effects, including swelling, burning or a skin infection.

It seems that attitudes to tattoos are changing, but they aren't quite there yet. Should you be persuaded to have one – visit a reputable tattoo artist with a portfolio. Discuss your design with them and don't make a hasty decision! If you later regret it, your tattoo will need laser removal or a cover up. Better get a temporary tattoo or henna tattoo first and see if you're happy with it. Wear it for a few months and then decide.

vocabulary.entry: tattoo /təˈtuː/ n. 纹身；刺青
vocabulary.example: She got a small tattoo of a butterfly on her wrist.
vocabulary.translation: 她在手腕上纹了一个小小的蝴蝶纹身。

vocabulary.entry: go under the needle /ɡəʊ ˈʌndə ðə ˈniːdl/ 接受纹身（口语）
vocabulary.example: He finally plucked up the courage to go under the needle.
vocabulary.translation: 他终于鼓起勇气去纹身了。

vocabulary.entry: tattoo parlour /təˈtuː ˈpɑːlə(r)/ 纹身店
vocabulary.example: There's a new tattoo parlour opening in the town centre.
vocabulary.translation: 市中心有一家新的纹身店要开业了。

vocabulary.entry: controversial /ˌkɒntrəˈvɜːʃl/ adj. 有争议的
vocabulary.example: The new policy is highly controversial among the public.
vocabulary.translation: 这项新政策在公众中极具争议。

vocabulary.entry: commemorative /kəˈmemərətɪv/ adj. 纪念性的
vocabulary.example: They issued a commemorative stamp to mark the event.
vocabulary.translation: 他们发行了一枚纪念邮票来纪念这件事。

vocabulary.entry: sleeve /sliːv/ n. （手臂的）半袖纹身；全袖纹身
vocabulary.example: He spent a year getting a full sleeve tattoo on his left arm.
vocabulary.translation: 他花了一年时间在左臂纹了一个全袖纹身。

vocabulary.entry: celebrity /səˈlebrəti/ n. 名人；明星
vocabulary.example: The celebrity was surrounded by photographers at the event.
vocabulary.translation: 这位名人在活动现场被摄影师团团围住。

vocabulary.entry: visible tats /ˈvɪzəbl tæts/ 可见的纹身（tats为tattoos的口语缩写）
vocabulary.example: The company now allows visible tats in the workplace.
vocabulary.translation: 这家公司现在允许员工在工作场所露出纹身。

vocabulary.entry: relax a ban /rɪˈlæks ə bæn/ 放宽禁令
vocabulary.example: The government decided to relax the ban on Sunday trading.
vocabulary.translation: 政府决定放宽对周日营业的禁令。

vocabulary.entry: individuality /ˌɪndɪˌvɪdʒuˈæləti/ n. 个性；个人特质
vocabulary.example: She values her individuality and refuses to follow trends.
vocabulary.translation: 她珍视自己的个性，不愿跟风。

vocabulary.entry: cultural heritage /ˈkʌltʃərəl ˈherɪtɪdʒ/ 文化传承；文化遗产
vocabulary.example: We must protect our cultural heritage for future generations.
vocabulary.translation: 我们必须为后代保护好我们的文化遗产。

vocabulary.entry: withdraw /wɪðˈdrɔː/ v. 撤回；撤销
vocabulary.example: The company withdrew its job offer after discovering his criminal record.
vocabulary.translation: 公司发现他有犯罪记录后，撤回了工作邀请。

vocabulary.entry: protected characteristic /prəˈtektɪd ˌkærəktəˈrɪstɪk/ 受保护的特征（法律术语，如性别、种族、宗教等）
vocabulary.example: Age is a protected characteristic under employment law.
vocabulary.translation: 根据劳动法，年龄是受保护的特征。

vocabulary.entry: breach /briːtʃ/ v. 违反；违背
vocabulary.example: He breached the company's dress code by wearing jeans to the meeting.
vocabulary.translation: 他穿牛仔裤参加会议，违反了公司的着装规范。

vocabulary.entry: dress code /dres kəʊd/ 着装规范
vocabulary.example: The restaurant has a strict dress code – no casual wear.
vocabulary.translation: 这家餐厅有严格的着装规范——不允许穿便装。

vocabulary.entry: infection /ɪnˈfekʃn/ n. 感染；传染
vocabulary.example: The wound became red and swollen, showing signs of infection.
vocabulary.translation: 伤口红肿起来，显示出感染的迹象。

vocabulary.entry: reputable /ˈrepjətəbl/ adj. 信誉良好的；受尊敬的
vocabulary.example: We only deal with reputable suppliers to ensure quality.
vocabulary.translation: 我们只与信誉良好的供应商合作，以确保质量。

vocabulary.entry: portfolio /pɔːtˈfəʊliəʊ/ n. （艺术家、设计师等的）作品集

vocabulary.translation: 这位纹身师给我看了她之前的作品集。

vocabulary.entry: hasty decision /ˈheɪsti dɪˈsɪʒn/ 仓促的决定
vocabulary.example: Don't make a hasty decision – think about it carefully first.
vocabulary.translation: 不要仓促做决定——先仔细考虑一下。

vocabulary.entry: laser removal /ˈleɪzə rɪˈmuːvl/ 激光去除（纹身等）
vocabulary.example: Laser removal of tattoos can be painful and expensive.
vocabulary.translation: 激光去除纹身可能既痛苦又昂贵。

vocabulary.entry: temporary tattoo /ˈtempərəri təˈtuː/ 临时纹身
vocabulary.example: The children had temporary tattoos of dinosaurs on their arms.
vocabulary.translation: 孩子们手臂上贴着恐龙图案的临时纹身。

vocabulary.entry: henna tattoo /ˈhenə təˈtuː/ 彩绘（临时纹身的一种）
vocabulary.example: She got a henna tattoo on her hand for the wedding.
vocabulary.translation: 她为了婚礼在手上画了一个彩绘。

sentences.english: Do you have any tattoos?
sentences.chinese: 你有纹身吗？

sentences.english: I don't.
sentences.chinese: 我没有。

sentences.english: I've never been brave enough to go under the needle.
sentences.chinese: 我从来没有足够的勇气去纹身。

sentences.english: But if you do have one, you are not alone.
sentences.chinese: 但如果你有，你并不孤单。

sentences.english: According to a report by Experian, the number of tattoo parlours in Britain increased by 173% between 2004 and 2014.
sentences.chinese: 益博睿（Experian）的一份报告显示，2004年至2014年间，英国的纹身店数量增长了173%。

sentences.english: Tattoos have always been controversial – personally and culturally.
sentences.chinese: 纹身一直颇具争议——无论是在个人层面还是文化层面。

sentences.english: Some people love them and some hate them.
sentences.chinese: 有人喜欢，也有人厌恶。

sentences.english: So, are they good or bad?
sentences.chinese: 那么，纹身究竟是好是坏？

sentences.english: These days, one in five people in the UK has some ink – whether it's a commemorative date, a sleeve or a full body suit.
sentences.chinese: 如今，英国五分之一的人都有纹身——无论是纪念日期、半袖纹身还是全身纹身。

sentences.english: What's responsible for this rise in popularity?
sentences.chinese: 是什么让纹身如此流行？

sentences.english: "You see a lot of celebrities getting tattooed," says Lee Clements of the British Tattoo Artist Association speaking on BBC radio.
sentences.chinese: 英国纹身艺术家协会的李·克莱门茨在BBC广播中表示：“你会看到很多名人纹身。”

sentences.english: As a result, people want to copy them or it becomes a fashion thing – certain tattoos become a trend.
sentences.chinese: 因此，人们想要模仿他们，或者纹身成为一种时尚——某些纹身图案会成为潮流。

sentences.english: Employers have become more accepting of visible tats too.
sentences.chinese: 雇主们对可见的纹身也变得更加宽容。

sentences.english: Last year, London's Metropolitan Police relaxed a ban on recruiting candidates with visible body art.
sentences.chinese: 去年，伦敦警察局放宽了对招聘有可见纹身候选人的禁令。

sentences.english: And earlier this year, Air New Zealand said it would end a ban on body art to allow workers to express their individuality and cultural heritage.
sentences.chinese: 今年早些时候，新西兰航空表示将取消对纹身的禁令，允许员工表达自己的个性和文化传承。

sentences.english: That said, not all employers would agree.
sentences.chinese: 尽管如此，并非所有雇主都认同这一点。

sentences.english: Grace, 28, told the BBC that she had been offered jobs in sales, which were then withdrawn when employers saw her hand tattoo.
sentences.chinese: 28岁的格雷丝告诉BBC，她曾获得过销售岗位的工作机会，但当雇主看到她手上的纹身后，offer被撤回了。

sentences.english: "It feels like having a tattoo is not socially acceptable," she says.
sentences.chinese: “感觉纹身在社会上是不被接受的，”她说。

sentences.english: "Having a tattoo does not amount to a protected characteristic," remarks Susan Harris, legal director at the GMB union, a UK trade union.
sentences.chinese: 英国工会GMB的法律总监苏珊·哈里斯表示：“纹身并不是受保护的特征。”

sentences.english: This means a person can be dismissed for having one if it breaches the employer's dress code – except on religious grounds.
sentences.chinese: 这意味着，除非出于宗教原因，否则如果纹身违反了雇主的着装规范，员工可能会因此被解雇。

sentences.english: And let's not forget the risk of infection.
sentences.chinese: 此外，我们不要忘记感染的风险。

sentences.english: At present anyone in the UK can set up a parlour and offer procedures without proper training, a report from the Royal Society for Public Health says.
sentences.chinese: 英国公共卫生学会的一份报告称，目前在英国，任何人都可以开设纹身店并提供纹身服务，无需接受适当的培训。

sentences.english: They note that just under 20% of those tattooed experience negative side effects, including swelling, burning or a skin infection.
sentences.chinese: 报告指出，近20%的纹身者会经历副作用，包括肿胀、灼痛或皮肤感染。

sentences.english: It seems that attitudes to tattoos are changing, but they aren't quite there yet.
sentences.chinese: 人们对纹身的态度似乎正在改变，但还没有完全转变。

sentences.english: Should you be persuaded to have one – visit a reputable tattoo artist with a portfolio.
sentences.chinese: 如果你被说动想要纹身——一定要去找有作品集、信誉良好的纹身师。

sentences.english: Discuss your design with them and don't make a hasty decision!
sentences.chinese: 和他们讨论你的设计，不要仓促做决定！

sentences.english: If you later regret it, your tattoo will need laser removal or a cover up.
sentences.chinese: 如果之后后悔了，你需要通过激光去除纹身或者覆盖纹身。

sentences.english: Better get a temporary tattoo or henna tattoo first and see if you're happy with it.
sentences.chinese: 最好先纹一个临时纹身或彩绘，看看自己是否满意。

sentences.english: Wear it for a few months and then decide.
sentences.chinese: 几个月后再做决定。
